PUSS AND THE KITTENS. Our old eat has kittens three— What': do you think their names ehosild be! One is a tabby, with emerald eyes, And a tail that's long and slender, And into a temper she quickly flies If sou ever by chance offend her. I think we shall call her this-- I think we shall call her that; Now, don't you think " l'epperpot" A nice name for a cat? One is klack, with Oral of white, And her feet are all white fur, ton; If you stroke her she carries her tail upright And quickly begins to purr, too. I think we shall call her this— I think we shall call her that; N )vr, don't you think " Sootikln" A nice name for a cat? One is a tortoise shell, yellow and blaek, With a lot of white about him; If you tense him, at once he sets up his back; He's a quarrelsome Tom, ne'er doubt him. I think we shall call him this— I think we shall call him that; Now, don't you think " Scratchavray" • A nice name for a cat? Our old cat has kittens three, And I fancy these their names will be: , Pepperpot," " Sootikin," Scratchaway "—there: Were ever three kittens with these to compare? And we coil the old mother—now, what do you think! Tabitha Longclaws Tidleywiuk. --Tom. Hood.

On roesaticaing the deputies, he found that they wanted to be paid weekly instead cf fortnightly, but they also wanted the fortnight's wages weekly. " sYny, me lads," exclaimed the astonished employer, "you are demanding exactly _ donate wages!" "Hoots, no sir I" replied one of them. "It's slaust as mere or lees than the same wages, put you mast shust paid us twice as fast as evermore." - No SOONER Shan THAN DorrE.—Jeremy White 0113 Of Oliver Cromwell's domestic chaplains, paid his addressee to Lady Frances, the Protector's youngest daughter.' Oliver we told of it ler a spy, who followed the matter so closely, that he hunted by to the lady'e chamber, and ran imme- diately to the Protector with this news. Oliver, in a rage, hastened thither himself, and going in hastily found Jerry - • on his knees, ;timing the lady's hand. In A fiery he asked what was the meaning of that posture before his daughter. White said," May it please your highness, I have a long • time ceurted that young gentlewoman there, my ledy'e woman, and cannot prevail; I wee therefore humbly pray- ing her ladyship to intercede for me." The Protector, turn- ing to the young woman, cried, " Whae's the meaning of this, hassey ? Why do you refute the honour Mr. Vildis Would (lo you? He is my friend, and I expect rag should bleat him as such." My ledy's woman, who desired nothing more, with a very low curtsey, replied, "If Hr. White in- Janda me that honour, I shall net be against him." "Say you so, my lass ? " cried Crornesell ; "call Goderyn ; this business shall be done Presently, before I go out of the room." Mr. White had gone too far to retreat; the parson came, and Jerry and my lady's woman were married in the pretence of the Protector. Tate LANCASHIRE OPERATIVES AND THEIR CHILDREN.— 'Unlike tire puddlers and furnacemen of South Staffordshire, . who seek compensation for their hard work in sumptuous fare, the diet of the operatives is neither wholesome nor nietritieue. In the larger proportlon of cases, a properly cooked dinner is a luxury only seen once a week; while tea, being convenient to carry and °ant to prepare, is the staple article, with such relish to the tread as a rasher of bacon way give. Tht', children at school Come oft no better than their parents at the ; and in the home only one meal a day is partaken of by the family together, except on Sun- day. If the people of Lincashire are degenerating physi- cally, some of the causes at least will be found in the facts -- here etated. Yet there is no lack of money, and in no part of the country are excarsione and picnics more common, with all the other signs cf a rough plenty arising from large earnines. Our gigantic manufactuse is doill2 something worse than that which Mr. Reeltin deplores—defacing our lever landscapes by its great chimneys and their black smoke, poltating the rivers and poisoning the fish—it is eating slowly hut surely into the home life of the nation, elating the children of the working claws on the street, motherless and fatherless in all respects but the name, set- ting a task to weekday and Sunday school.; they cannot se- CDT plish ; and it is doing all this in the name of trade, and thrift, and industry—a terrible sacrifice, covering our boasted civilisation with el-;anae.—Good Words., COURTSHIP AND NARRIAGS.—With an honourable girl— With -an honeureble men—an engagement carries with it Something more than a few sunny months of courtship. After owartehip comes tnirriege. After marriage comes the home. To describe the reetors which to some young people seem quite sufficient to justify them first in flirting and then in getting " engaged " would answer no good purpose. Bet —putting aside the indirect manner in which writers addrece their readers—let me rpnik frankly to you as a friend to a friend. Let me ask yen to =sides what you mu 4 have in your future husband, in your future wire, to -- sleeks it even tolerable to spend twenty or forty years to- gether. I will not inelet on the elements which are neces- sary to the romantic perfection cf married life, for most of us are commonplace people, and a life of romance is beyond Oar reach. There are some very commonplace things you Ought to make sure of. Good, sound health is one thirg; %here are twenty grave moors for insisting on it. Next to this I should put perfect truthfulneed ; the man who will lie to other people will lie to his wife; the girl who will lie to ether people will lie to her hushaand. Next to truthfulness —temperance, Industry, and courage. Then fortitude; that is, the power be hear pain and trouble without whin- lug. Then utiselliehneer ; for the selfish man, the selfish girl, though drawn out of selfishness in theearly weeks of ec'art-glip, will settle hack into it again when the wear and worry of life come on. I said just now that most of us arc commonplace people, and that a life of romance is out ef our reach, belt I believe ht" falling in love." The imagina- tion should be kindled and the heart touched; there should he enthueiesm and even romance in the happy months that precede marriege, and something of the enthusiasm and ro- mance should remain to the e vehryappeinndmofanlidfeg,roareee.lseTthhee home is wanting in its perfect wonderful charm which makes the wife more to the husband than all other women, and the husband more to the wife than all other man; this is neoessarw tea happy marriade. A. brmerod for the Royal Agricultural Society.- They are six in number, representing the large white cabbage butterfly, the turnip-fly, the beet-fly, the wireworm, the hop-aphis with lady-bird, and the daddy long-legs, with the grubs and pup of each. PAPER SACKS FOR FLOUR.—Benjamin Smith, of Canajo• harie, N.Y., the pioneer in the paper flour sack industry, said:—" In 1860 cotton advanced to such a price that a 6-cent fl...er bag cost 35 cents., and something had to supply the place of the older material. The most expert paper manufacture-A couldn't supply me with paper that met the requirement& It would crack or tear. But at last, in 1862 or 1863, I got a mepilla paper that would do, and in the latter year turned out the first flour sack ever made of paper." As showing the growth of the industry, Mr. Smith said that between 1861 and 1870 paper flour bags were made and sold at the rate of 60,000,000 per year, at an average price of from 50 to 100 dollars per 1,000, and during that period cotton sacks would have cost 150 dollars per 1,000. This was a seving of 5,000,000 dollars. In ten years, ke- tween 1870 to 1880, the country took 100,000,000 paper flour sacks per year. One thousand paper flour bags have about the same bulk as a barrel, but the 1,000 bags will hold 250 barrels of flour.—St. Louis Miller. SIZIZIIRE FOR TITHES.-1 correspondent vouches for the truth of the information that the Rev. W. D. Elingstone Vicar of Farnborough, Kent, has just seized forty-nine sheep under dittraint for tithe. The sheep were the prbperty ot Mr. James Goodman, of Tenterdeo, who had pat them out to graze on a Farm in the occupation of Mr. E.l". Browning, of Farnborough.' Mr. Browning, through adverse seasons, wet unable to pay his tithe, and the reverend titheowner took the opportunity afforded him of making another man pay up for his debtor. I have said that the sheep were the property of Mr. Goodman. They are so still morally; but legally they belong to the Christian minister whpee peetoral Instincts were too strong for him to resist the temptation of adding to his flock. This, apparently, is his idea of "gather- ing sheep within the fold."—Mark Lane Express. A ti;ffi nelty bae long been experienced in marking polled cattle, and many have been opposed to cutting the ears of animals. The Rev. John Gillespie, editor of the Gelleway Llerd Book, and Mr. Cranston, of Eolstane, have been making experiments with a process of tattooing the ears of cattle, which they recommend. They use a machine with fine lance points shaped into figures and letters, and the numbers can be varied up to 9999. This machine pierces the ear, and immediately after the wound is rubbed over with Ineien or other permanent ink. When the wound is healed, the numbers are as legible as the tattoo marks on a sailoi'e arm or breaet. If this process were applied to dog's eve; it would probably spoil dog etealing. Profeeeor Buckman has published in Bell's Weakly Mes- a valuable paper on diseased grasses in the produc- tion of abortion in cattle. The paper is based upon ob• servations made chiefly during the late summer on a farm in Dorsetshire where the farmer had suffered heavy losses. The professor gives a list of over twenty grasses which he found ergotieed, and states that grasses affected with ergot or other :ongold diseases will be liable to make cattle abort. "Taking these matters, then, into consideration," be says, "and the damp state of the atmosphere, especially in Dorset- shire, for the last few eoars, we feel perfectly convinced that the miserable condition which has occasionally occurred in Dorset in the last-few years is entirely due to the diseased condition of the grass, &ought on from an extra state of atmospheric moisture." What a capital argument in favour

of drainage. It is somewhat perplexing to a stranger on first visiting England and going among the flock-masters there, to hear the different names applied to sheep of different ages. Thy call a ram lamb a tap, a heeder, a purlamb, a hog, a hogget, a hoe,gerel, a lamb hog, a tnp hog, a teg. Afeer being shorn he is called a shearing, a shearling, a shear hog, a diamond or diemont ram or lisp. After the second shearing he is a two-shear ram or tap, and on the third year a three-shear ram, ti:s. The female is a ewe or gimmer lamb ante' weaned, and then a gimmer hog or ewe hog or teg or sheeder ewe. After being shorn she is called a shearing ewe or gimmer, a theave or double-toothed ewe or teg, and after this a two shear, Sic. Btrren ewes in some of the northern districts are. called eild or yeld ewes. How much more simple and precise is our American nomenclature—a Lamb, a yearling, a two-year-old.—An Old Flock-master. THE HAY TRIALS AT READING.—The letter Of Mr. W. A. Gibbs seems to necessitate my encroaching upon your space so far as to state that I am in no respect responsible for the action of the Royal Agricultural Society with regard to the wording of the offer of my prize, or with regard to the conditions which were attached to it for the guidance of the judges. I merely offered the money as a prize for hay- dryers, and stated at the time that I should be quite satis- fled with any terms which the Council thought fit to make in regard to it. Under these circumstances I cannot be ex- pected to enter into a newspaper correspondence even with any actual competitor for the prize, much lees with one who, like Mr. Gibbs, did not -enter at all. I had hoped, however, that the good work done by one of Mr. Gibbs' natchines on the sewage farm adjacent to the trial fields (work which even the much-abused judges mention favour- ably in their report) would have been considered by your correspondent as publicly and sufficiently proving the great use and value of his method under conditions lees onerous and exacting than those necessarily obtaining In the society's triele.--3fartie J. Satton. rho extension of the employment of machinery in egri- culture AS a counterbalance to the lack of hands is thespre- dominant question just now for French farmers and the National society fel. the Enc naragement of Agriculture have resolved to devote their annual congress held during the Paris agricultural exhibition to this question. The sitting will be held at the Hotel Continental on the 25th, 26h, and 27th January next ; and the chief topic for discussion will be-1. A Home Ivies "BROKEN WlND."—Horsos with "thick* or "broken" wind will frequently werle for a lung period if jodiciouely treated, and ills well to. bear in mind that more can be done to relieve the animal by proper dieting than by the administration of medicines. It is nearly always found that broken-winded horses are also the subject of indigestion or flatalence. Care meat be taken to prevent overloading the stomach and bowels, and with this object all coarse or woody foods, damp or musty hay and corn should be care- fully withheld. The food, which should be of good nutri- tive value and given regularly, inuat always be damped, either with water or treferably with boiled linseed tea; a few ounces ,(eight to twelve) of linseed oil can be given from time to time mixed with the food or in the form of a draught. Broken•winded animals should, where practic- able, be moderately fed and watered about two hours before being called upon to work, more especially when used for driving. Precautions should also be taken to prevent over- gorging when the animal is returned to the stable. For medicine, arsenic given in small doses once or twice daily and continued during several days, or even weeks, is fre- quently of aervice ; whilst mineral tonics, as sulphate of iron, diluted hydrochlorie acid, &c., give tone to the stomach and assiet digestion. One of the most eminent Scotch vete- rinarians, whose fame in treating broken-winded horses was widespread. used in addition to advising careful dietetic measures, to prescribe balls of the following composition : Thirty grains each of calomel, digitalis, opium, and cam- phor. Where the medicine was to be persisted with daily for a week or longer, the calomel was omitted after the first or second dose. For the upright joints, a mild cantharidee blister, repeated once or twice; will be found beneficial, and when striding in the stable the horse should have his legs enveloped in cold, wet bandages, applied with a moderate degree of tightness. " num BATH CISARMS "—I hope your readers will notice the assertion of" Rob Roy" that Ills well known" to the initiated" that, in order to get a fall day's work out of any Scottish work-oxen, the driver must be one " who can sing or whistle to them" at times. Ido not in the least doubt the truth of the statement; but I should like to hear if Shorthorn ox teams are equally alive to the influence of sweet sounds, and I should like to know if " Rob Roy'e" ex- perience states whether instrumental is equally efficient with vocal music; and if it makes any difference if there is but one tune and set ef words all day, or if 'variety is found to urge on the flagging team. And it seems to me it is highly desirable to ascertain how -Ur:this peculiarity of giving extra wages to a ploughman who can sing and whistle explains the old Scotch saying, "A penny for your whistle." When Jenny Lind first made.her appearance in our cotin- trr, I remember an old farmer expressing his great disgust at some neighbours who had gone to hear her. Ha, how- ever, carefully gave ins to understand that to music, in itself, he had no objection. Music In a concert room was, in his judgment, music thrown away. "I mind," he said, "when you could always tell whether the cows were got up by hearing the gala a-singing. When I was young, there TM Do-and-so von could hear singing as she milked half a mile off. Ah ! and those cows used to give out'—that is, increase their flow of milk—most uncommon." Possibly musical boxes will -come into ordinary farm practice, like artificial manures.—Greybeard,in Agricultural Gazette.

SCIENTIFIC NOTES. PLaNrs FOR PAPER-MAKING.—Dr. George King, super's- tendent of the Royal Botanic Gardens, Calcutta, has bees making fresh experiments on the commercially as well as scientifically important subject of plants suitable for paper fibre, which appear in his report for 1881-3. He has been expodmentmg chiefly on the plantain fibre, and from what he says it seems that during the dry months simple expo• sure of the sliced plantain stems is a sufficient preparation for the paper maker, provided the paper mill is on the spot. What is still wanted is some cheap mode of removing the us. Bless cellular tissue, so that the fibre may be shipped to England without the risk of fermentation during the voyage. Dr. King is very decidedly of opinion that from the cultiva- tion of the plantain for its fruit being so universal over the warmer and damper parts of India, and from its growth being so rapid, the conversion into a marketable commodity cf the sterts At present thrown array as useless would lie an apareci.,alt addition to the wealth of the country. HARD AND Sorr WA-fut.—The hardoess or softness of a wat.r dtptnds zpou the amount of mineral ingredients

div.head: EXAMINER SATURDAY, DECEMBER 9, 1882.
div.p: THE EXAMINER SATURDAY, DECEMBER 9, 1882.

which it contains. These mainly consist of carbonate and sulphate of lime, the former giving rise to what is called temporary hardness—it being for the most part removable , by continued boiling, whereby it becomes encrusted as chalk I upon the inside of the vessel in which the wnter is boiled; and the latter to permanent hardness, because it is not thus removable. A. very hard water is injurious for drinking purposes, because its power as a solvent for food is impaired, and because it is absorbed by the stomach with greater difficulty than a soft water, thus giving rise to indigestion or dyspepsia. In addition to the long train of distressing I symptom! which are included under tae term dyspepsia, 1 there is strong evidence to prove that the habitual drinking of very nard water also gives rise to goitre, a disease associ- ated in many places with that fearful form of idiocy known as cretinism. In many parts of England goitre is found to to prsvail only in those districts where the magnesium lime- stone formation is abundant. In some districts of Switzer- land the use of certain spring waters of unusual hardness has been followed by the production or augmentation of the dis- ease in the course of a few days, and similar results have fre- quently been observed in India.—Good Words. •

DEATH OF THE PRIMATE. The death of the Archbishop of Canterbury took place on Sunday morning, at a quarter past seven, at his residence, Addington Park, Croydon. The Primate passed away quietly and apparently free from pain, in the presence of his children and a few others. Throughout the whole of Saturday, and up to the time of his death, his Grace was in A semi-unconscious condition. He last spoke on Saturda night, having uttered a few words in reference to an attac of spasms which he felt was impending. He died on the day which lee regarded as the Anniversary of his wife's death four years ago. On Friday, Lady Ely visited the Archbishop with a message from the Queen. His Grace attempted to write a reply to Her Majesty, but what he wrote was not legible, except his signature ; and the mes- sage was written by his son-in-law, Mr. Davidson, In alrubst every church in the kingdom reference was made from the pulpit to the great loss which the Church of Brig- ; land has sustaing,d in the death of the Archbishop. i "Men of the IYme " says that Dr. Tait was the youngest i son of the late Craufurd Tait, Esq , W.S., of Haryieston, county Clackmannan, his mother being A daughter of the late Sir Islay Campbell, Bart., of Succoth, sometime Lord President of the Court of Session, born in Edinburgh, Dec. 22, 1811, was educated at the High School and at the Acedemy at Edinburgh, under Archdeacon Williams; went in 1827 to the University of Glasgow, where be attended the lectures of tile late Sir Daniel K. Sandford and Mr. Buchanan; was elected in 1880 an exhibitioner en Snell's foundation, to Balliol College, Oxford, of which he became successively Scholar, Fellow, and Tutor, and graduated BA. in first-class honours. He subsequently became a Public Examiner of the University. Whilst residing at (Word in his capacity ascollege tutor, he took a prominent part in opposing the spread of Tractarian principles, and was one of the °four tutors who first drew the attention of the university authorities to the celebrated Tract No. 90, written by Mr. Newman, for the purpose of showing that the Thirty-nine Articles of the Established Church could be henestly subscribed by those who held Roman Catholic doctrines. His opposition, however, to this school of theology, always courteous and open, was marked by the most sincere respect for, and personal attachment to, those who held these peculiar views. The circumstance of Mr. Tait being in holy orders proved, in the then state of the law, an obstacle to his appointment, in 1838, to succeed the late Sir D. K. Sandford in the Greek chair at Glasgow; but the death of Dr. knold, in 1842, opened to him a field of greater usefulness, as he was serected to fill the important office of Head blaster of Rugby School, where he remained eight years. While there he married a daughter of the late Venerable Archdeacon Spooner, brother of the late Mr. Richard Spooner, loeg one of the members for Warwick- shire, and uncle of the then Bishop of Oxford. A severe illness, occaeioned by over-exertion in his arduous post, pro- bably induced Dr. ;Fait to accept from Lord John Russell's Government, in April, 1850, the deanery of Carlisle. But, to a man of his mental activity and conscientious devotion to his sacred calling, this could be no post of indolent retirement. He originated, and generally conducted himself, an additional pulpit service on Sun- days, besides undertaking an amount of labour in visiting the poor, instructing the young and ignorant, and superintending the public charities of a large town, seldom equalled by the most hard-working parish clergyman, and was at the same time an active member of the Oxford University Commission. The late Dr. Blom- field having resigned the see of London, under a special Act of Parliament. in August, 1856, Dr. Tait was nominated to the vacancy. In 1863 he proposed, and by his zealous efforts powerfully contributed to the successful initiation of, an extensive scheme for supplying the deficiency of church accommodation in London, by raising a fund of £1,000,000 in the course of ten years. On the death of the late Dr. Longley, in 1868, Dr. Tait was appointed his successor in the archiepiscopal see of Canterbury. The University of Glasgow conferred on him the degree of LL.D. in 1869. Dr. 'Fait has written two volumes of sermons preached either at Oxford or in the school chapel at Rugby • a work entitled "The Dangers and Safeguards of Modern Theology," with remarks on the celebrated "Essays and Reviews," pub- lished in 1861; the "Word of God and the Ground of Faith," in 1863 ; Charge to the Clergy in 1886; and has contributed articles on education and kindred topics to the Edinburgh and Nora British Reviews. The family of the late Archbishop declined the proposal that the Primate's remains should- be interred in West- minster Abbey, and the funeral took place yesterday (Friday) at Addington Church, where the deceased prelate's wife and son are buried.
HOUSEHOLD PETS.

DOC/S.—THE Wiesrire.—The mastiff is cue of the oldest of our English breeds, and there is a traditional interest about it which no other breed possesses. The mastiffs of Lyme Hall and Chatsworth were the earliest known speci- mens, anesome of the best dogs of the day have mucti of the blood in them. In fact the possession of the Lyme Hall breed is So jealously guarded that few have succeeded in obtaining specimens of it, and fierce controversies have raged as to whether certain doge are descended from this breed. The story of how a mastiff saved the life of one of the Leighs of Lyme Hall, and how out of gratitude the breed has bean and is still preserved in its purity, it is not necessary to repeat here. A well-bred mastiff, if thoroughly broken, is an excellent companion for a lady or gentleman, and quite sufficient protection to any one taking a lonely walk if ride, and as the temper and disposition of the mastiff are quiet aud gentle, he seldom or ever leads his owner or himself into any unpleasant collisions with man or beast, while the presence of her noble pet inspires the most timid lady with confidence as to her safety, whether site be in the house or out el it. The size and powerful frame of these dogs are sufficient to deter the most determined ; and as some dogs reach 150 and up to 170Ibs. in weight, they make very formid•ahle antagonists. The head of the mastiff should be short, flat, and broad, quite square at the muzzle, the latter to be very black ; the eyes seould be dark grey or brown in coloticr, small, deep set, and placid in their ex- pression, neither fierce nor yet sad-looking; the neck should be short, muscular, and well set on W the throat clean, with- out any loose flesh about it; the girth of the chest is better the greater it is, and no dog should measure less than 40 inches at that point; the feet and legs should be straight and well-formed, and like those of the greyhound or fox terrier ' • the feet as round as a cat's; the colour is generally a light fawn, with black muzzle, eyes, brows, ears, and toe nails, but some are to be found of a brindle colour ; the loins ought to he wide and thick through ; the coat fine, close, and short ; the tail rather long, but strong, straight, and muscular. Good specimens sell for very high prices, and ten guineas as a stud fee or for a very young ptippy is not considered at all out of the way. Mastiff puppies require a great deal of liberty, exercise, and the best of food to bring them to the size and appearance required, and if these points are not attended to they become stunted, the legs weak, bowed, and out of proportion, the feet flit and shapeless, and the dog, instead of being an object of admiration, is ugly in the extreme, certainly not fit to be kept in any house or to be the companion of any lady of gentleman. • CATS.—YZEDING —IS is very important, in order to keep a cat in good condition, that it be fed regularly, and have sufficient food. some are not trained to be honest, but many that would be honest if they could are thieves from neceasity. A cat ought to be fed twice a day, and it is much better to have a proper dish for her put down at proper times and removed when the meal is finished. Oatmeal porridge in milk, or bread and milk, to which a little sugar has been added, are very good for breakfasts, but for dinner or supper she should have an allowance of flesh. Boiled lights are very good for this purpose, but a little fish should also be given occasionally, and in feeding teach the cat to wait patiently until she is served, which can be done by the I exercise of a little skill and patience. If you want her to be nice and clean treat her now and then to a piece of fresh butter, as this acts as a laxative, but she also uses the grease, mixed with her saliva, as a kind of soap for cleansing her coat. Above all, do not give a cat too many tit-bite at the table, as meat in excess is apt to cause diarrheas, and there is no means of gauging the quantity given in this way. Feeding between meals is certainly a very bad practice. PIGEONS—THE HOMING INseitacr.—We left off last week after seeing what course the birds take when liberated. We must now see what would be the horizon visible to the pigeon from the height at which he determines the direc- tion of his flight. But to do this it is necessary to calcu- late what this height would be. Signor Chapins justly aeserte that, in order to elevate itself to a height at which it would disappear from our sight, it must ascend about a mile and a quarter. Now physical science teaches us that an object illuminated by the daylight does not disappear from our sight till it has reached a distance of nearly three thousand five hundred times its diameter and we may thus assume that a pigeon does not rise much .more than half a mile before it decides upon the direction it will take, as it Is perfectly visible to us when it does so. From what has been observed as to the range of vision from mountains, it is probable that at this height, unless broken by mountains or other natural barriers, the pigeon can, upon a clear day, discern objects two or three hundred miles away. This would be of no use were there not other qualities as well, for a homer mast have intellectual power to apace,. .ate localities, and it must also be able to recognise positions ab- stractedly or relatively, and, of course, it must have a strong sense of sight, for only by this can objectrf at a distance be appreciated. That there is some other sense, as yet undis- covered by man, and probably undreamt of by him, Prat- most a certainty, for birds have been known to reach their homes during a dense fog, when it was impossible to see ten , yards. A well authenticated Case proves this; and in another instance, a bird was bought in Belgium, brouget to England, where it had never been previously, but by a mis- take on the part of its purchaser it obtained its liberty, and found its way back to Belgium in a few hours. As it would be able to view sea on both sides when it rose, yet knew not any of the ground, we are baffled to know how it could settle upon the right direction. Upon this question we give the following extracts from "Noses on Cage Birds" (Bazaar Office, London) —' It is certain that our birds die of ailments in captivity which never attack them in a wild state; and, theegh we may never altogether prevent, we are most likely to diminish these by diversity of food, and by natural medicir e—if I may so call it—such as cuttle fish, a bone of which I always keep suspended by a wire on the walls of my aviary. For the standing slishers of soft-billed birds I supply a mixture of egg (yolk, 'white, and shell chopped up together), crushed hemp, and, In the winter, a few grocer's currants, German ants' eggs, ;ind grated carrots; when fresh ants' eggs are not to be had, a tin of bread and milk sop, and a plate with a little finely- cooked meat. All these will be partaken of freely by the , .other birds, the two latter by the parrots and cardinals espe. daily. For luxuries (some of which I give every day when they are to be found, and when not, mealworme) ; spiders, earwigs, beetles, caterpillars, grubs, moths, little worms, and indeed every insect the garden affords. The house-flies, caught in the ordinary fly-trap, washed thoroughly well and dried in a cloth, are quickly snapped up by the insect-evorm birds; wasp grubs, and aphis-covered twigs also find favour. An ants' nee, dug bodily up, and placed in a shallow box in the aviary, will afford a sup Ply of ants, their eggs, and larvae for a week, if it be judicially broken up a little and turned over every day. OPENING OF THE NEW LAW COURTS. In fine weather and amid every sign of public interest on the part of .the people of London, the Royal Courts of Justice were on Monday opened by the Queen. The fact that her Majesty was to open the building in person stimu- lated the desire for admission to such a degree that ordinary peers and members of the House of Commons had to be con- tent to ballot for the hundred And fifty tickets with which both Houses had to be satisfied, while the Corporation of the City of London had to distribute as best they might only thirty tickets But the gathering was as representa- tive as it was select, Ministers and ex-Ministers' the Diplomatic Body, the Army and Navy, and the Civil Service, the clergy and learned professions, and, as a matter of course, the indica' bench-and the bar, all contributing to the splendour of the assembly, while the ladies who were privileged to be present gave additional colour and interest

to the scene. All traffic in tile Strand and the thoroughfare from Pad- dington Station was stopped from about 10 o'clock, and the streets were thronged with dense crowds. The judges, in their state robes, headed by the Lord Chancellor, the Lord Chief Juetice, and the Master of tele Rolls, drove from West- minster to the new courts about 11. The procession of the civic dignitaries invited to the ceremony arrived from the Mansion House about noon. Her Majesty, who was accom- panied by Princess Christian and Princess Beatrice, left Windsor at 10-55, and travelling by the Great Western Rail- way, arrived at Paddington at 11.30. The route taken was by way of Constitution Hill, past Buckingham Palace, along the Mall, out by the Stable-row-gate, past the western end of St. James's Palace, into Pall-mall by Cleveland-row, and by wr,y of Duncannon-street into the Strand, where snore particularly the decorations were numerous and elaborate, the Apecteitors were packed in dense masses, and the popular welcome was especially marked. On arriving at the Central Hall the Queen, who had had been joined by the Prince of Wales, the Dukes of Con- naught, Albany, Cambridge, and Teck, and the Duchess of Teck, was received by the Lord Chancellor, the Judges, and the Ministers. The First Commissioner of Works (Mr. Shaw-Lefevre) formally intimated to her Majesty that the new edifice, the rearing of which had occupied eight years, was now ready to be devoted to the administration of justice. He then formally handed the key of the structure to the Queen, who, by the Home Secretary, passed it to the Lord Chancellor. Her Majesty then read a short address, in which she expressed her trust that the uniting together of the various branches of judicature in this the supreme court would conduce to the more efficient and speedy discharge of justice to her subjects, and- that the learning and inde- pendence of her Judges would prove in the future, as in time past, the chief security of the rights of her crown and the liberties of her people. The Lord Chancellor, in accept- ing the trust impoeed upon him, dwelt upon the legislative improvements which had distinguished the present reign, and especially upon the cansolidatioe and union of the several branches of the Legislature. A special prayer having been offered by the Archbishop of -York, the Home Secretary, at the Queen's command, declared the courts open. 'Next an address was presented to the Queen by the Prince of Wales on behalf of the Inns of Court ; and Her Maeeety acceded to a request made by the Attorney-General that the proceedings of the day should be entered on the records of the Supreme Court. The Treasurers of the Inns of Court were presented to Her Majesty, and several of the judges in succession. "God sevethe Queen" was played as Her Majesty's procession passed out into the Quadrangle, and the company were "played out" by selections from Le Prophete. When the company was dispersing, and forensic, military, court, and fashionable costumes mingled in the broad crimson carpeted aisle, there was thus created a brilliant dissolving view which was not the least interesting of the spectacular events of the day. After receiving an address from a repre- sentative body of workmen who had been engaged upon the building, Her Majesty was conducted to her carriage, and drove to Paddington Station amid the most loyal demon- strations, and then returned to Windsor. The Court appeared in mourning on account of the death of Arch- bishop Tait.

TRADE NOTES. A general strike of the miners of Northumberland threatened. The existing sliding scale for the regulatio, of wages is about to expire, and a new scale offered by tilt masters has been rejected by a vote of the men. It is announced that the toalowners of Lancashire and Yorkshire vcil: in short time withdraw the ten per cent. ad- vane° iu prices which was imposed last month. The reduction is said to have been forced apon the owners by a considerable falling off in the demand. „ Tw LANCASUIR 'acne TRADM—A nominally steady tone is maintained in the iron market, but prices remain unaltered simply because makers abstain from pressing sales. Buyers who still believe that prices will have to give way place out only such small orders as are required to cover pressing necessities, and to effect sales of any importance lower prices than those now current would have to be taken. There was little or no business stirring on 'Change on Tues- day, and prices Meli scarcely be said to be tested. Lance, makers were still gdotirig ,Ds to 50s, less 21, for forge and foundry pig iron delivered equal to Mancnester, and district brands were quoted at from 49s to 50s for Lincoln- shire, up to 50s and 525, less 2, for Derbyshire; but sales could not be made at these figures, and any transactions reporteel appeared to be conflued to odd lets which could be bought at under current rates. For finished iron there has been a very limited inquiry, but although some of the makers are in want of orders, there is not much disposition to give way, and £6 103 remains about the average price for local bars delivered into the Manchester district. THE LANCASIIIRB COAL TRADE.—The coal trade generally of this district continues only dull, with many of the pits not working more than four days a week. Some of the col- lieries have larger quantities of slack on hand than they can deal with, but generally supplies of good engine fuel are not excessive. In the Manchester district the list rates are without alteration, and although here and there some un- derselling is reported, this has not been to such an extent as to necessitate say giving way on the part of the leading firms upon the advance. During last month a good many concessions of from 6d. to 04. per ton were made on round coal, and these with the commencement of December have become pretty nearly general. At the pit mouth the average prices are now about 103. to 103. 6d. for best coal, Sc. to 83. 6d. for seconds, and Os. to 7s. for common round coal, according to quailty. Engine fuel remains without material change, good bargy averaging 4s. 94. to ss. at the pit, and good slack 3s. 6d. to 35. 0,1., with bast sorts fetching in some cases 4s. to 4s. 3d. per ton. Shipping continues only dull, and deliveries at the kigh level, Liverpool, or at Gars- ton docks, steam coal can be bought at Bs. to Bs. 3d., and seconds house coal at 98. to 93. 6d. per ton. Tern LABOUR MARKET.—The labour market remains in a fairly satisfactory condition, and at most of the leading centres of industry there is at least an average amount of employment. At Birmingham business is fairly goecl, but in several branches French; Belgian and German competi- tion is again complained of. At Wolverhampton the manu- factured iron trade is still well supplied with orders, and at Sheffield the heavy branches are very busy, and many of the lighter trades brisker towards the approach of Christ- mas. At the leading northern ports iron shipbuilding and marine engineering remains very busy. Steelmakers at Barrow-in-Furness are fairly well employed. In Northum- berland the miners have decided to discontinue the sliding scale in the adjustment of wages. At Newcastle-cn-Tyne trade generally is fairly brick. The textile branches show no important changes, but at Bradford spinners complain much of want of orders. At Kidderminster the . manufac- turers are fairly supplied with contracts, and at Leeds the chief firms are tolerably well employed. At Leicester the hosiery trade is somewhat quiet. Several important rail- way, dock, and other works are still in progress, and at some points good hands are in demand. Emigration is for the present somewhat slack, but the Government of South Australia continues to offer special advantages to good agri- cultural labourers, some classes of mechanics, and domestic servants. The colony of New Zealand is also advertising extensively for the last-mentioned clase.—Labour News.

THE STATE OF IRELAND, A special commission will be issued to try the prisoners charged with the Abbey-street murder. The commission will consist of three judges, who will sit without a jury, in accordance with the provisions of the Crimes Act. ANTICIPATIONS Or DISTRESS.—At a meetiag of the Evicted Tenants' Fund, commenced in Cork on Saturday, reports were received of indications of ipiminent distress throughout the country. Several speakers said the country will be in a worst state during the coming winter than in the past two years. ANOTHER CONSTABLE SHOT.—On Saturday evening, a constable, named James Donohan, was fired at and severely wounded near the police station at Coolacoonsy, and within a few miles of Tubbercurry, county Sligo. The outrage is not supposed to be agrarian. Captain J. Gage, RM., took Donohan's depositions, but the police have not as yet suc- ceeded in arresting kis assailant. THE MAAMTRAINA TRAGEDY.—The arrangements for the execution of the men condemned for the Maamtrasna murders are being completed at Galway Gaol, the scaffold having just been erected. On Wednesday, the mothers and other relatives of the condemned men visited them, and the interview was most affecting. The prison is guarded night and day by a strong force of soldiers. Unless any reprieve be granted, the eight condemned men will be executed simul- taneously on the 18th inst. The winter assizes for Ulster were opened on Wednesday at Belfast, and Mr. Justice Harrison' in charging the Grand Jury, referred with satisfaction to the small calendar, only 55 prisoners being in custody from a district embracing one- third the population of Ireland. The number of crimes reported 'had also fallen in the twelve months from 357 to 201, and that was a most satisfactory statement when the condition of the metropolis and other districts was con- sidered. The Commission Court at Dublin was on Wednesday en- gaged in trying a serious case of agrarian crime Thomas Behan, labourer, was indicted for setting fire to the dwelling- house of a farmer who had " ventured " to take possession of a farm which had become vacant. The evidence, was wholly circumstantial, and apparently not sufficiently con- vincing for the jury, who were finally discharged without agreeing. Mr. Justice O'Brien expressed his surprise at the result, and, whilst ordering the prisoner to be detained in custody, said he had his own opinion as to where the plot to burn the house was planned. EXCITED SPEECH BY THE NEW M.P.—An Irish demon- stration was held on Monday night in Salford in aid of evicted tenants in Ireland. Mr. O'Donnell, M.P., who was the principal speaker, said the government of Ireland was founded on nothing but an organisation of force, and he challenged the Government to get the verdict of an English jury against him for saying that Mr. Kenny, M.P., said he was prepared to repeat on Irish soil the statement for which the Government had indicted Mr. Healy, and if the people of Ireland were so foolish as to expose themselves to starva- tion by paying their rents to robbing landlords the verdict of every coroner's jury should be Serve them right." JUDGE O'BRIEN ON THE STATE OF CRIME.—The Dublin Special Commission was opened at Green-streeeCornmieeion Com t, at eleven o'clock on Monday morning, before Mr. Justice O'Brien. The grand jury having been sworn in, Mr. Justice O'Brien addressed them, alluding to the numerical decrease of crime in the country, the decrease consisting mainly of the cases of threatening letters and notices. There was not, however, the learned judge remarked, any decrease in the amount of undetected crime, as the recent attack on Mr. Justice Lawson, the murder of Constable Cox, and the attempted assassination of Mr. Field would show. Mr. O'Brien further alluded to the effect the increase of such offences was having on the trade of the city, which was gradually decaying from those influences, and everyone who was able to give up his business was doing so, and fleeing from the city as if it were infected by the plague. AN " INFORXER " AT GLASGOW.—An extraordinary state- ment has been made to the Glasgow police by an Irishman named Macmillan or Demper. He was refused admission to a lodging-house on Saturday evening, and, while the police were taking him to the station for shelter, he stated that be could put them on the track of the men who attempted to assassinate Mr. Field. He said thst he lived in Greenock, in the same house where the hired assassins lived "like lords." Doubt being expressed as to the truth of his state- ment, he asserted that It was not the first time that he had been asked to murder a man ; " but added that he always refused to "go for any one." Since then he has several times repeated his story, and vouches for its truth. The Irish Constabulary have been communicated with. Mr. Redmond, M.P., writes denying that Mr. William Redmond, his brother, had gone to the Continent in order to avoid the consequences of his recent speech at Cork. He says that for five days after the Cork meeting Mr. William Redmond remained in Ireland.. He then started for the south of France, to which place he had been imperatively ordered by his doctors for the benefit of his health, which was well nigh shattered, first by imprisonment under the last Coercion Act, and more recently by a six weeks' fever in New York, from which he is only slowly recovering. It was not until his arrival in Paris that he first heard he was to be honoured by a State prosecution. This he is quite willing to face; but, acting in accordance with the urgent wish not only of myself but of all his political friends and leaders, he will not to suit the convenience of the Govern- ment, alter his previously-arranged plans, but will remain In a warm climare'until his health is restored. MR. DAYITT BEFORE THE JUDGES.—There was consider- able excitement in the vicinity of the Dublin Four Courts, on Tuesday, when Mr. Healy, M.P., Mr. Devitt, and Mr. Quinn appeared before the judges in answer to a summons taken out by the Crown counsel to sliow cause why they should not be bound over to keep the peace or be committed to prison in respect of their seditious language at a recent meeting. No progress was made in the trial, an application by the defendants for an adjournment which would enable them to prepare their replies being readily granted. The case will come on again in ten days. At the Commission Court, in Green-street, Mr. Justice O'Brien delivered his charge to the Grand Jury, who subsequently found true bills against the three men charged with the murder of Lord Ardilaun's bailiffs b_r drowning them in the Laugh Mask. The prisoners were arraigned, but on the plea that some of their important witnesses were absent the trial was fixed for Thursday. Thomas Curran was also indicted for the murder , of Henry East, who he is alleged to have shot in the county Roscommon, but here again a postponement was applied for and conceded, the prisoner being returned for trial at the next Commission. The Grand Jury have found true bills against the threb men in custody for the murder of Con- stable Cox, and against the man who attempted to shoot Mr. Justice Lawson in the streets of Dublin. THE CASTLEISLAND SHOOTING CASE.—The 18 prisoners who were arrested on suspicion of being implicated in the recent shooting affair near Castleisland, were brought up on ,

Saturday, before Mr. Hefferman Considine, R.M. Ten were discharged, as there was no evidence likely to compromise them, and the remaining eight were remanded. The pri- soners were conveyed to the county gaol at Tralee under a strong escort on Saturday night. The wounded police- constable now lies in a critical state at the Tralee Infirtriary, whither he was removed on Friday. The bullet, which ap- pears to be a revolver one, struck him above the chin, and lodged in the side of his head. His version of the attack shows that a most formidable attempt was made to destroy the whole party. He states that as they approached a poin of the road where a lane intersects it they heard a whistle and immediately afterwards a rustling noise behind the hedges at each side. The moment they, keard the noise both sides of the road became lit up by a blaze. At least eight or ten shots must have been fired at the same moment, and they heard bullets whizzing past them, lie was struck under the mouth, and fell stunned, but recovered after a few minutes. Sub-Conetable Kerr fired four or five shots at the party from the road, and then went into the field. When he recovered sufficiently he joined Kerr in the field, and attempted te fire his rifle with hie left hand, the other hand having become disabled in the fall, but failed. -Kerr doritinued to fire in the direction that the assailants had taken. Kerr thinks that one of his shots took effect, for he heard one of the men moan. Boyle had a six-chambered revolver in his pocket, but he did not use it, and remained standing in the road. Kerr pursued -the men, and entering a house about 200 yards from where the shooting took place, arrested three men he found there. Edward Boyle, the man whose assassination was primarily tke object of the assailants, has ben in the employment of Lord Ventry as rent warner and gamekeeper, and two attempts were made before on his life.

FoREIGN INTELLIGENCE. One hundred persons have been iujured and one killed cutright by a railway accident on the Melbourne and Hob- son's Bay line in Australia. Malappo's successor, Jonathan, has had a fight with his rival Joel, in Basutoland, and defeated him, capturing his town. The Executive Council of the Free State has met to consider the situation.

A young Englishwoman named Julia Bentley has been found strangled in a house at-Florentina, a short distance from Madrid, where she had lived for twelve months as a governess. The occupier of the house, a Frenchman named Gainez, has been arrested. A shocking tragedy is reported from the village of Scho- newalde, near Konigsberg. On Thursday night a woman of that place, in a fit of insanity, threw her three children into a deep well at the back of her dwelling-house. She then it fire to the out-buildings, and afterwards herself leaped into the well, from which next morning four corpses were taken out.

The inquiry into the circumstances connected with the ease of the Cuban refugees has terminated. It has been decided that the Colonial Secretary and the Chief Inspector of Police cannot be permitted to retain their offices, and that though the acting_police magistrate, who was not dis- charging his regular duties, must be severely censured for his conduct. the Secretary of State does not feel com- pelled to remove him from his office of Captain of the port of Gibraltar. THE UNITED STATES REVENUE.—The annual report of the United States Treasurer glows that the revenue for the year was $42,000,000 in excess of that of the previous year, and that the expenditure decreased by nearly $3,000,000. The debt has been reduced by more than $166,000,000. The gold in the Treasury has decreased by $23,000,000, and the silver increased by $26,000,000. The report states that the circulation of the banks is the greatest ever known, and is tufficient to meet all except speculative demands. It is stated that there are indications of an approaching discussion of the entire fundamental principles of the entire banking system. The news from the Transvaal through Durban is a little more sanguinary than usual. The Caffres have been driven into the caves of Mapoch, a cave has been destroyed by dynamite, 50 natives have been killed, many cattle have been captured, and according to the native accounts Mapoch has been completely and finally defeated. Another cor- respondent, alluding teethe daily skirmishes on the Trans- vaal frontier, states that the Boers are nearly always successful. The arrangements in progress at Natal for the return of Cetewayo are not likely to be complete before the close of the year. There is a general opinion in Zululand that there will be fighting when Cetewayo returns.

EXTRAORDINARY SCENE IN A PRISON: CONVICTS DRIVEN AT THE POINT OF THE BAYONET--The last arriving mail from Australia brings pat ticulars of a desperate scene which was witnessed inside the yards of the convict prison at Par- ramatta, when, what was undoubtedly intended as a rising en masse of the prisoners was averted by tha prompt and decisive action of the authorities, though the convicts themselves bad to b 3 driven at the point of the bayonet into their cells. According to the information it would appear that the action of the convicts was the result of a precon- certed arrangement. The prisoners were scattered in the four yards of the gaol, and when they were ordered to leave afid go to their cells they refused. The officials at once saw that a rising was impending and immediately sent for assis- tance. A number of police arrived, but it was not until they had fixed bayonets that the convicts were made to obey The orders of theiwarders. The scene while it lasted AT TER was a desperate sue, even when the men had been fastened in their cells they gave vent to yells and screams of the PRE STON GUILD, wildest description. Subsequently a furt'ler reinforcement SEPTEMBER, 1882, of men arrived at Paranaatta from Sydney, as it was ex- pected that the convicts intended another outbreak. No B 6 mention was made of any of the mutineers having been I.7.INGER'S SEWING IT rt injured, but it appears it was only the determination of the RE CEIVED authorities to put down the revolt in the strongest way that made the convicts desist from their intention. THE HIGHEST AWARD. EGYPT. THE SENTENCE OF ARABI. The court martial met at Cairo on Sunday morning, it having been arranged that the charge against Arabi should simply be rebellion, and that the accusations of massacre ' and incendiarism should be abandoned. The prisoner, acting on the advice of his counsel, pleaded guilty. The ' court then adjourned to considei its judgment. On reas- sembling sentence of death was passed. This was at once commuted by a decree of the Khedive into banishment for life. It is understood that Arabi's place of exile will be some British colony or possession,upon parole, but with sufficient supervision to prevent his escape. Before the court-martial and sentence Arabi expressed a wish to live free at Damascus, with his children, keeping aloof from political

- affairs as long as he is out of Egypt ;but if the Sultan and Moslems would not permit his dwelling among the Moslems then he had a preference for London. Since the sentence he has written a letter in which he says he shall cheerfully proceed to any place which England may be pleased to ap- point for his residence, and remain there until the day comes when it will be possible for England to modify her opinion concerning him. He has a conviction that in a short time English people will be able to realise the fact that his rebellion had a very strong justification. He then hopes, when the English people have finished the work which he commenced, to return to his country and see with , his own eyes the result of her humane and civilising work. He expressed his gratitude to Mr. Gladstone and Lord Granville for their interposition on his behalf, and to Lord Dufferin and Sir E. Malet for the, kindness and generosity they had shown him. He slso thanked the British people and the great English press, which was.unauimous in de- mantling that he should have a fair trial, and says he shall leave Egypt with the firm conviction that, as days pass by, the justice of his cause will become more and more apparent.

EXCITING SCENE AT THE ST. • HELENS RAILWAY STATION. NARROW ESCAPE FROM DEATH. A most exciting scene was witnessed on Wednesday night at the St. Helens station of the London and North-Western Railway. On the arrival of the 4.34 train from Liverpool the attention of the stationmaster was called to a man in a third-class carriage whe was causing some disturbance, and who said he wanted to go to St. Helene. Mr. Moss informed him that he had arrived at his destination, and requested him to leave thf train, which he did, but on alighting he became like an " infuriated tiger," rushing wildly about the platform and striking at every railway official he came to. Foreman-porter Harvey appears to have been the first within his reach, and the man struck him violently several times, knocking him down. He then aimed at several others near, but missed them, and rushed at the stationmaster. Mr. Moss dodged the blow, and the man fell head first from the platform on to the rails over which his body lay. Just at this moment the Southport train was steaming into the station, and; Mr. Moss shouted loudly for the driver to stop. While this was going on, Harvey, who had got up, jumped into the four-foot to the assistance of the man, but bad barely time to tarn him round a little and jump out of the way. when the Southport train, which could not be stepped, oame up. The man at this moment was lying in a slanting direction, his legs being close to the platform, the other half of his body and head inside the rails. Had the train been coming at a good speed, the man must have been literally Cut in two, but as it was he was caught by the guard of the engine and pushed bodily out of the way. When the train was stopped a number of officials dragged the man to the platform, when he again commenced his violent conduct and struck wildly at everybody. Even Harvey, rho had saved the man's life at the risk of his own, was again ill- treated, and one porter had his hand bitten. Eventually the man was tripped up, and on the arrival of Police- constable Addison was handcuffed, and placed on one of the company's handcarts and taben to the lock-up. On Thurs- day morning prisoner was brought up before Alderman Har- rison. He gave the name of John Riley, and said he had yesterday landed in Liverpool by one of the West Indian Pacific Co.'s steamers from America, on board of which he had acted as fireman. He was charged with being drunk and assaulting a foreman porter, named James Harvey, in reply to which he said, "I suppose lam guilty." As there was only one magistrate present, formal evidence was taken, and prisoner was remanded.

The experimental tunnel boring on the other side of the Channel has now advanced to the extent of ba f a mile from the bottom of the shaft. It is stated that the amount of water encountered is gradually diminishing as the heading advances.

William Newton, a Birmingham labourer, was at that town, on Tuesday, committed tor trial at the Warwick Assizes for causing the death of his brother, by kicking him 5o violently when on ths ground that death shortly after- wards ensued. The prisoner and deceased had, previously been quarrelling respecting their wives.

div.head: tUE PROROGITION OF PARLIAMENT.
div.p: tUE PROROGITION OF PARLIAMENT.

THE QUEEN'S SPEECH. Parliament was prorogued on Saturday. In the House of Lords the Royal Message was read by the Lord Chancellor as follows : khr LORDS A/CD GENTLEMEN— , After a session of remarkable duration I at. at length inabled to bring your labours to a close. I continue to hold relations of cordial amity with all foreign Powers. The commercial negotiations with France, which were proceeding in the month of February, did not result in the conclusion of a treaty. But the Government and Legisla- ture of that country have pursued an enlightened policy, aM there has not in consequence been any general falling °ftiLl ths dealings between the two countries, which at ?ace promote their material well-being and strengthen the °ands of friendship now happily uniting them. The operations in Egypt, both naval and military, which a wise liberality enabled me to conduct upon an adequate scale, and which were prosecuted with such energy and fidelity in all the departments, were brought to an early and successful issue_ I take this opportunity of placing upon record my grati- tude to the able officers who commanded by sea and land and to the victorious forces, of which ray Indian army supplied a distinguished part. The recent events in Egypt have enhanced my obligatiok in regard to its affairs, of which I spoke to you at the begin- ning of your protracted session. I shall study to discharge my duties in such a manner as to maintain international engagements, to uphold and con- solidate the privileges which have been zuccessfully acquired, to promote the happiness of the people and the prudent development of their institutions," and to avoid any measure which might tend towards disturbing the tranquility of the East. And I feel confident that my aims, and the result of my counsels, will commend themselves to the approval of the Powers, my allies, in their several relations to that intereet- ing region.
GENTLEMEN OF THE HOUSE OF COMMONS- I thank you for the supplies which you have granted me to meet the various and extended wants of the pane service

MY LORDS AND` GENTLEMEN— After a succession of unfavourable seasons in the greater Portion of the United Kingdom, the produce of the land has, during the present year, been for the most part abundant, and trade is moderately active. The growth of the revenue, however, is sensibly retarded by a cause which must in itself be contemplated with eatis- faction. I refer to the diminution in the receipts of the exchequer from the duties on intoxicating liquors. In some parts of Ireland I am compelled to anticipate distress during the approaching winter. I hal e alsa to record with deep pain that the horrible crime of assassination has been rife in the metropolitan city of Dublin; and there is s special call of duty upon the executive authority to exercise with fidelity and firmness the powers with which it has been entrusted, In the social condition of the country at large, however, I have the satisfaction of noting that there has been a marked improvement; and the law has acted with renewed Vigour under the provisions you have devised. I have an earnest hope that this improvement will be maintained and extended. I am indebted to your wisdom for having passed the Measures which I deemed indispensable for restoring the supremacy of the law in Ireland, end for removing impedi- ments_ to the wide and progressively enlarged action of the Land Act of 1881. `. You have also passed a Yariety of measures from which, in their several spheres of operation, I anticipate much advantage to my people. I could, indeed, have desired to coneratulate you at the Present time on your having been able to meet the wants of the country for practical and effective legislation on many well-known and weighty subjects of high interest to large Portions of the community, some of which I commended to Your notice at the opening of the session. After the recess, you will resume your labours under cir- cumstances which, I trust, may prove more favourable to their accomplishment than those of the current year; and I rely with confidence on your energy and wisdom for the discharge, under the Divine blessing, of the arduous respon- sibilities which must ever attach to the Parliament of my empire. The Commissioners then raised their hats, and the Sj)eaker retired frem the bar with the members by whom he had been accompanied. The Commission proroguing Parliament to Thursday, 15th February, was then read, and the proceedings termi- nated at half-past four o'clock. Amongst the members of the House of Commons who attended with the Speaker at the bar of the House of Lords were Mr. W. E. Gladstorfe and Lord Randolph Churchill. In the commons, several notices for next session were given, and questions asked in reference to the Cuban refugees and Arabi Pasha's trial. The House was then summoned to the House of Lords to hear the Queen's Speech read. On returning to the Lower Chamber, the Speaker read the Royal Speech, and then took leave of Mr. Gladstone and and the other members present, as they filed past his chair. 'rue session was then at an end.

HARE AND HOUNDS. CHESHIRE TiLLY-ECO OLUD. - Fifteen members went to Liverpool on Saturday to take part In a run with the Wirral' Harriers, whose head-quarters are at Higher Tranmere. It was four o'clock before the pack, which numbered twenty-nine, started from the Victoria Hotel, and once clear of the houses and out in the open country, they timid to their discomfort that they had to face a bitterly c'ild wind and driving rain. The shelter afforded by the woods at Stara:on was found very acceptable, and after about a mile of heavy going the ru .nets reached Storeton village. From this place the trail led straight back to Tranmere, over a good deal of ploughed and pasture land, and up the hill to Prenton, the finish being along Prenton Lane and the Borough Road. In spite of the darkness during the latter part of the run, no difficulty was experienced in keep- ing the trail, and the pace, considering the number of runners, was very well sustained.
