The case of Bradlaugh v. Newdegate was before the Queen's Bench Division, or Saturday. It came up on de- murrer by the plaintiff to the defendant's statement of , defence in the action. Mr. Justice Field directed that the questions raised by the demurrer should await the result of the trial of the issues iavoired in the action, and gave judg- ment accordingly. The official volunteer returns for the year which ended on October 31 have been received at the War Office, and it is now possible to indicate the general results. It appears that there will be a falling off of at least 5,000 on the total of 208,000 which was reached last year. Efficiency has, how- ever, vastly increased, and there are numerous other evi- dences to show the increasing vitality of the organisation. EXPLOSION AT A MlLL.—Shortiv before breakfast time on , Tuesday, one of the high-pressure cylinders at Coldurst Mill, , Oldham, was blown into fragments, which were scattered in all directions' detholishing the windows. Fortunately, no one was in the engine-room at the time. The mill is a limited concern, and upwards of one hundred operatives will be stopped by the breakage. General Sir Drury Lowe arrived at Chirk, North Wales, on Wednesday, on a visit to Lord Trevor. An address of welcome was presented, and in reply the General denied the accuracy of a recent statement as to the manner in which the battle of Kassassin was won. Hr repeated emphatically that the charge of the Household Cavalry, directed solely by the Egyptian masketry, brought about the enemy's defeat. POISONING CAS E AT NOTTINGH&M.—Mr. Brown, coroner, on Wednesday, concluded a lengthened inquiry as to the death of Mrs. Whillance, of New Stapleford, Nottingham, wife of a colliery engineer, who was poisoned by arsenic contained in a dose of magnesia. The medicine was pur- chased at a shop in the village, and given by the purchaser to deceased, whose husband took some and was very ill. The Jury considered the affair accidental, but could find no evidence how the arsenic was mixed with the magnesia. THE QUEEN AND THE MALAGASY ENTOYS.—It is stated that at the Cabinet Council held on Monday it was decided to advise the Queen to grant the request of the Malagasy envoys for an audience, and that her Majesty has signified her willingness to receive them early next week. The docu- ment handed by the Malagasy envoys is largely historical, extending back to 1504, when, it states, the first Europeans landed in Madagascar. It recounts all the subsequent com- munications held with foreign Powers in order to combat the French pretensions to any portion of Madagascar. The envoys have been invited by the Fishmongers' Company to a banquet on the 14th inst. Tun MISSING SCOTCH ACCOUNTANT.—Tho investigations into Mr. D. S. Peddie's defalcations in connection with the fnnds of the Friendly Society of Dissenting Ministers of Scotland was reported to a meeting of the Directors, held at Edinburgh on Wednesday, by Mr. J. Knox Crawford. The result of the invcstigation is that of the capital fund of £29,000 only £5,000 remains secured, so far as yet ascer• tamed. A meeting of the society is to be called for an early day to receive the agent's report and take such measures as may be deemed necessary in the interests of the society and its beneficiaries. We have to report a number of disasters consequent upon the heavy gale which visited the east coast of England and Scotland on Monday night. A brig, named the Catherine and Mary,/ of Sunderland, founded when near Tynemouth Pier, and all hands perished. From the north come accounts of losses sustained by the herring fleets, several men haying been drowned by the sinking of fishing boats. Numerous vessels have been driven ashore at various points en the coast, but in the majority of instances the lifeboats have saved the imperilled seamen. Lk the Midland Counties and North Wales there has been a heavy tall of snow. THE NOMINATION AT LIVERPOOL. The nomination of candidates for the representation of Liverpool took place at noon on Wednesday, in the Town Hall. Mr. Samuel Smith (the Liberal candidate) was the first to be nominated, and he was proposed by Mr. S. B. Guoin and seconded by Mr. B. D. Holt, and eight assenting burgesses also signed the paper. Mr. Smith was also nominated a second and third time. Mr. A. B. Forwood, the Conservative candidate, 'was proposed by Mr. Edward Lawrence and seconded by Mr. Edward Whitley, M.P., there being nine assenting burgesses. Mr. Forwood was also nominated a second time. Both candidates, as they

MISCELLANEOUS. A man named Palmer dropped dOwn dead in the Salis- bury market on Saturday. Major Greig, C. 8., late head constable of Liverpool, died at Broad Sayes, Bournemouth, on Saturday evening, aged 75. Miss Sarah Apted, a native of Reigate, and now living at Redhill, on Saturday reached the age of 100 years. She was one of the three who started the first Sunday school in Reigate. A telegram from Glasgow says that Lord Balfour, erincipal Tulloch, and others, in order to counteract the action of the -Dissenting party at the next general elec- tion, have started a Church of Scotland Defence Aseocia- tion. A general order was issued by the Field Marshal Com- manding in Cfsief on Monday, intimating that the services of those men of the first-class army reserve who were called out on permanent service in July last are no longer required. Whilst a man was crossing the Great Northern Railway, near Lincoln, on Saturday morning, he was knocked down by a train, the whole of which passed over his body, literally cutting it to fragments. A dense fog prevailed at the time. Mr. Justice Groves gave judgment, on Saturday, in the action brought against Messrs. Waring Brothers, contrac- tors, by Mr. Adam Murray, as trustee of the separate estate of Mr. Jonathan Nield, formerly a partner in Fenton's Bank at Rochdale. His lordship ordered the return of the sum of £3,000, subject to any damages which the defendarits might have been entitled to when 'the contract was broken in January, 1870. He thought the amount of damages ought to be only nominal under the circumstances. MRS. LANGrRY'S PHOTOGRAPHS IN TONS—The London Stereoscopic and Pnotographic Company have just completed an order for 200,000 portraits of Mrs. Langtry and Madame Patti for the proprietors of Pear's Soap, who intend them for free distribution throughout the United States. The weight elone of this consignment amounts to no less than four tons, and is the largest order of the kind ever executed. The portraits are produced by a permanent process, and the mounts bear the testimonials given to Messrs. rears by these ladies. NEW KNIGHTS.—In connection with the opening of the Royal Courts of Justice, on Monday, her Majesty has not only conferred the dignity of an earldom upon the Lord High Chancellor, but has also beetowed the honour of knighthood upon the following gentlemen: Mr. John P. de (lox, Q.C., treasurer of Lincoln's Inn; Mr. John Blossett Maule, Q.C., treasurer of the Inner Temple; Mr. William St. James Wheelhouse, Q.C., treasurer of Gray's Inn; Mr. Tesmas Paine, president of the Incorporated Law Society. Meal, Telma—Early on Monday morning a large mill in the occupation of Mr. J. Hoyle, at Longwood, near Hudders- field, was ahnest totally destroyed by fire. The damage to the building and its stock of valuable machinery is reckoned at £16,000, and 200 operatives are temporarily thrown out of employment. A similar disaster occurred on Monday after- noon at Horwich, near Bolton' whereby a mill worked by Messrs. Clark and Collins, of Manchester, was destroyed, the amount of the damage being £12,000. EXECUTION AT LIVERPOOL. Bernard Mullarkey, aged 19, labourer, was executed at Kirkdale Gaol, Liverpool, on Monday morning, for the murder of a fellow labourer named Thomas Cruise, by burning the loft in which he was sleeping, at Maghull, on September 25th. Since his condemnation Mullarkey has maintained an attitude of stolid indifference, though he is stated to have paid atten- tion to the ministrations of his priest. Representatives of the press were excluded from the prison at the time of the execution, but it is understood that, along drop having been given, death was instantaneous. Maresood was the execu- tioner. BURNING I WIDE wrna A RED-HOT POLAR: HORRIBLE CASE. On Monday, at Whitehaven Police Court, Robert Hodgson, Whitehaven, was charged with having burned his wife with a poker. The prisoner had made the poker red- hot whilst his wife was in bed, and then rubbed it over her throat and legs. Dr. Nance stated that the burns were four inches long, and deep. The prisoner's wife said he had been drinking, and it was partly the " horrors " that caused him to burn her. Prisoner, who had been previously fined for throwing boiling water over a person. was sentenced to six months' imprisonment. THE HON. IVO BLIGH'S AUSTRALIAN TRAIL -- A very decisive victory has been won by the English cricketers in a match concluded against the eleven of New Soueh Wales. The contest continued over three days, and was witneseed lay large and enthusiastic crowds. In their fi, et innings the Hon. Ivo Bligh's team succeeded in making the fine total of 461, to which Leslie was chief contributor with a splendidly compiled innings of 1.14. On going to the wickets the home team got 152 in their first innings, and having to follow on were all out for 165. Thus the Englishmen won by an innings and 144 runs. Mr. Parnell presided on Saturday at a banquet given in the Westminster Palace Hotel to Mr. A. M. Sullivan. on his return from America. Responding to a toast, Mr. Sullivan said the Irish in the Greater Ireland, numbering ten or twelve millions, were a power in the world which must be taken into account by anyone who had to deal with Ireland. Statesmen of this country had of late years perceived this fact. The Irish in America were anxious that there should be union at home under the leadership of Mr. Parnell.— Mr. Parnell said he never could understand why he should be the leader of the Irish people. Their keen sense and instinct on public questions and political movements enabled them to do without a leader, and, in fact, the leader was lead by the people. He saw no reason to fear that they would not continue to gain advantages for Ireland, and consolidate the influence of the people at home. Mr. Justin M'Carthy, M.P., Mr. Kenny, M.P., and others also delivered speeches. THE TERRIBLE TRAGEDY IN A THEATRE.—ThEi play in which the American actor, Frank Fra.yne, is reported to have caused the death of a young actress at Cincinnati appears to be closely akin to the' drama of life in the backwoods " entitled "David Crockett," in which Mr. Mayo, an American performer, made his appearance at the Olmypie Theatre three or four years ago. In the latter piece, which was desiened to thrill the spectator by the act of shooting with a rifle at objects placed near the head of one of the performers, not only Mr. Mayo, but a little boy belonging to the troupe, was permitted to undertake this feat, much to the alarm of nervous persons in the stalls. Suspicions were not unnaturally entertained at the time that it involved some sleight-of-hand, and was not really so perilous as it seemed; but it was well known to the initiated that success depended upon skilful aim. That skill enough can be ac- quired to repeat the trick with impunity many hundred times seems to be certain; but after this unhappy demonstra- tion of its danger it is to be hoped that dramas of the type ef " Si Slocum" and "David Crockett" will no longer be tolerated.—Daily iVews. THREATENING THE PRINCE OF WALES AND MR. GLAD- STONE—At Bow-street Police Court, on Monday, a man named John Crueden, aged 47, giving an address in Wilson- street, Gray's ,Inn Road, was brought before Mr. Flowers, in custody of Inspector Swanson, of the Criminal Investigation Department, Scotland Yard, charged with sending a letter threatening the Prince of Wales and Mr. Gladstone. The letter read as follows : 19, Wilson-street, Gray's Inn Road. Professed head of Liberalism, what benefit are you to the country ? Liberal indeed to those who are not in want but under your (Liberal) guidance, in what state are the hard- working classes in this country? Hundreds and thewands round the streets actually starving, but willing to work for a very small pittance. If I should come across you or the Prince of Wales, or any such who are petted with their thousands, wherever it happens to be, they would have a rough time of it, for I would not stand particular what I would do. So take this warning, for I don't care.—Jno. I. CRUNDEN." Inspector Swanson proved the arrest of the prisoner at the address given—a lodging house. He admit- ted having written the letter, and was remanded. SINGULAR PERJURY CASE..—A charge of perjury, which has occupied the attention of the Wem magistrates four days and created great interest in the county, was concluded on Monday night. On the 21st September the Rev, Alexander Benson, vicar of Loppington, was charged with shooting at a pheasant without license, on the 28th August. The chief evidence against him was given bv Thomas Goldsborougb, Chambre Vaughan, of Woodcote, near Loppington, gentle- man, and Mr. Woodward, who swo're that they saw Mr. Benson shoot at the pheasant. The case was dismissed. From subsequent statements of Woodward, who said Vaughan offered him .£2 to give that evidence, and Wood- ward's admission that he was on his way from Shrewsbury when the pheasant was alleged to have been shot, he (Wood- ward) was summoned on a charge of perjury. The case was tried on the 17th November, Woodward being commit- ted for trial. Mr. Benson then took similar proceedings against Vaughan, feeling his character was at stake, and the hearing commenced on Thursday week. Thomas Em- berton' farmer, said Woodward had told him neither he nor Vaughan had seea the pheasant shot, and that Vaughan had offered him £2 to swear he did. He said Woodward's evidence would not do him much good, and that " parsons were big game to shoot at, and that he had be car, fl." After a lengthened consultation the Chairman (the Hey. Sir William Honyman) said it was their leery painful duty to commit the defendant for trial at the assize& Bail was allowed, the defendant nAn and two sureties in £5OO. These wt ol at nce forthcoming. A LADY Ad U R.ER COACHMAN: SCANDALOUS DI,ORCH C4611,-4n 'tie Divorce Court, on Saturday, the case of HOW: 11, P.arnst and liamblyn was heard. This was a peti- tion by the husband for a divorce on the ground of his wife's adultery with the co-respondent. There was no defence.— Mr. Middleton was for the petitioner, who was married to the respondent on the 13th January, 1870. The petitioner is a retired officer in the army, and after the marriage be resided with his wife at West Combe, Somersetshire. The parties seemed to have lived very happily together. In April cf last year the petitioner was away from home, and when he returned he found that his wife was being attended by Dr. Hyatt, the family medical attendant. That gentleman having communicated to him that his wife was enceinte, he went to her bedroom and saw her. She admitted that such was the case, and that Hamblyn, the coachman, was the father of the child. She went down on her knees and asked the petitioner's forgiveness, which was refused, and soon after she went home to her friends, who lived near Bath, and the present suit was instituted. The petitioner was called, and stated that he and his wife lived very happily together up to this occurrence. The only words he ever had with her related to her too frequent visits to the stables. Hamblyn had been seven years in his employment, as coachman.—Othef witnesses were called—several in the establishment—who spoke as to the visits of the co-resPon- dent to the respondent in her room when the petitioner was absent, and also of her visits to the room of the co-respon- dent, which was in the stables.—After hearing the evidetece. the court pronounced a decree nisi, with costs.

ELECTRIC LIGIAING.—Mr. Chamberlain on Tuesday received a deputetion of representatives from nearly all the important Corporations of the United Kingdom. Their object was to get clauses inserted in all the Electric Light- ing Bills which would render it permissive, instead of obligatory, as at present, to use the electric light. Mr. Chamberlain said the evident feeling of Parliament was that no obstacle should be put in the way of the fell development of electricity, and he thought the spirit of the Act would not be carried out unless Corporations undertook an obligatory order with regard, at least, to a portion of their district. If that were done, he saw no objection to a permissive undertaking under certain conditions with respect to the rest of the borough. A FRENCHMAN nit Swaim OE A FORTUNE. At Bow- street, London, on Tuesday, Felix Auguste Piot was charged on an extradition warrant with fraud within the jurisdiction of the French Republic. The prisoner was a banker, carry- ing on an extensive business at Rheims, and 12 months ago he sustained heavy losses on the Steck Exchange. He ab- sconded, owing £4,000. He came to England, and corn- I menced business as a wine merchant, under the name of Forrest and Co., 59, Mark-lane. He was arrested on Mon- day by Inspector Moses and Sergeant Coniurst, of Scotland Yard, at 18, King's-road, Peckham. He said that he had lost £lB,OOO, and only owed the amount mentioned in the charge. Four bills of exchange were found upon him. He stated that he had come to England to make his fortune and pay his debts. He was remanded. BOY BURGLARS.—An extraordinary burglary case came before the magistrates of the Home Division of Kent at Canterbury, on Monday. Two boys, sons of a retired French captain, named Chaproniere; residing at Herne Bay, were charged with,entering a dwelling-house in that town and stealing a large quantity of wine, jewellery, and other articles,to the value of many pounds, the property of Mr. C. W. Courtney. The prisoners, whose ages are ten and twelve, on being confronted with the police-officer, who had after several nights' watching obtained a clue to the burglars, made a full confession. They produced all the stolen property with the exception ef a fan, which they had given to their father's domestic servant, and the wine, which they said they had drunk, and they showed him the broken bottles in the ashbin. They had obtained access to the house by breaking a window in an adjoining dwelling , whiah was unoccupied; they had visited the house every , night for a week (thee prosecutor and his family being absent), and, besides carrying off property, had committed serious damage to musical instruments and clocks. The Bench ordered a remand for further inquiries to be toads into what they described as a most shocking case. SERIOUS EXPLOSION IN A MILL.--On Monday morning an explosion took place in the chemical rooni of Grove Mill, Keighley, the property of Mr. Robert Clough, m. orsted manufacturer, which resulted in serious damage to the building, but was not attended with any loss of life. In the chemical room there are two large retorts used for mann- factnring purposes. Adjoining this room is the warping room in which there were several hands employed. At ten o'clock an explosion took place in the chemical room, blow- ing down the walls and lifting off the roof. The workmen employed in the room were severely scorched, and a Mr. g'i; who happened to be there, was also slightly burned. were attended to by Dr, .J. B. Berry. The others were able Three Of the workmen weft taken home, and their injuries ee to remain at work. In the warping room the utmost con- sternation was caused, but the workmen sustained no injury. The fall of the outer wall caused a steampipe connected with the boiler to break, and steam had Co be let off, mcessi- tating a stoppage of the whole of the werks. The damage is confined entirely to the chemical and the warping rooms. The explosion is attributed to an escape of liquid from one of the retorts. The injured men are progressing favour- ably.

The Vice-Chancellor of Cambridge University has I announced the vacancy of the Plinnean professorship of astronomy, through the death of Professor W. Challis, who was elected in 1836. in a series of lottery prosecutions at Manchester, on Thursday, the stipendiary magistrates inflicted heavl penalties. The principal was sent to prison for three months, and ordered to pay £25 costs besides; one of his servants was fined £l5, or a month; and several minor offenders were fined 40s. and costs each. The annual meeting of representatives of the great ericket clubs of the country was held at Lords, on Tues- day, when arrangements were made for the principal matches of next year. An important resolution was come to at Tuesday's meeting in regard to the appointment of umpires. No man is to act in that capacity in a match in which his own county is engaged. Early on Tuesday morning, the steamer Peruvian, inward bound from Quebec and Montreal, collided in the Crosby Channel with the. Clan liner Clan Maclean. The Peruvian, which was cut down to the water's edge amid- ships, was beached to the northward of the North Dock Lighthouse. All the passengers were landed in safety. The Clan Maclean was also badly injured. THE GREAT ROBBERY OF HUMAN HAIR.—The Birming- ham police have recovered £3OO worth of the human hair stolen from Messrs. Scaletter, merchants, Navigation-strett, Birmingham. The hair recovered had been disposed of to different hairdressers, at very low prices, viz., £6 worth of 132-inch flaxen for £3. Ernest Lodge, prosecutor's dis- charged clerk, arrested on suspicion, was on Tuesday further remanded. Philadelphia is just now excited over the capture of a band of grave robbers, who were caught with six bodies, in- tended for the Medical College, in their possession. An investigation shows that these ghouls had almost cleared one of our cemeteries of its occupants. The recovered corpses' have been identified. This capture was planned by some newspaper reporters attached to the Philadelphia Press, who carried it out successfully, as amateur detectives. The men captured are now in gaol, awaiting their trial. On Thursday morning, a shocking suicide was committed at Wolverhampton Police Barracks. Police-Constable Ben- nett, 23 years of age, has been ill some time, and attended by the police -surgeon. On Wednesday night he became worse, and early on Thursday morning jumped out of bed, ran downstairs into the kitchen, and locked the door. His father ran after him, and on bursting the door open, found his son dead on the floor, a table-kife covered with blood in his hand, and his head nearly severed from

the body. A special message, just received from Lloyds, states that during a heavy gale, on Wednesday afternoon, a large vessel was discovered ashore on the Hale Sand, off North Somercotee, on the Lincolnshire Coast, and before assistance could be rendered she went to pieces and all hands perished. A quantity of wheat and ship's planking have already washed ashore; also some papers marked ship Fiona, of Glasgow, with other wreckage. The iron ship Fiona, 1,450 tons register, laden with a cargo of wheat, from San Fran- cisco, left Falmouth for Hull, to discharge, on Sunday last. There is no doubt but that is the vessel which has been lost. Her crew numbered 40 hands all told. MUTH°, M. LOUIS BLANC.—A familiar figure in French politics has passed away. M. Louis Blanc, who for many years had been one of the chief exponents of Radical princi- ples to his countrymen, died at a quarter to nine on Wednes- day morning, at Cannes, aged 70. He had been in failing health fzr some time, and had thus been prevented from occupying the prominent place in affairs he once held. During the Empire he was exiled, and sought refuge in England, returning to his beloved France after the collapse of Louis Napoleon's power, but only to make way for a younger generation of statesmen. DEATH or MR. TROLLOP.—Mr. Anthony Trollope's ill- ness has, as it was feared it would, proved fatal. He died on Wednesdaysat the age of sixty-seven. He was engaged, as is well known, for a lengthened period in the General Post Office, and while there wrote a considerable amount of fiction, which obtained for him a deserved and widespread popularity. His novels are legion, some of the best known being " Framley Parsonage,' "Orley Farm," "Can You Forgive Her ?" "'The Small House at Allington," "The Last Chronicle of Barset," " Phineas Phinn," and "He Knew He was Right." He also contributed to various magazines and other publications. His works were not of a sensational character, nor wokahe a deep thinker, but he presented many attractive studies of social existence, and was perhaps most at home in describing clerical life, of which he has left many pleasing pictures. The great snowstorm of Wednesday was most disastrous in its effects. In Scotland not only is railway traffic largely blocked by accumulations of snow, but outlying towns and villages are completely beyond reach, and several cases of death from exposure have occurred. Trains in all directions were "snowed-up" throughout Wednesday night, and one train which left Festiniog for Bala on that evening was only discovered on Thursday night embedded in a drift. Two passengers and three officials were in the carriages, and suf- fered terribly from cold and hunger. Great exertions are being made by the Postal Telegraph Department and the varidus railway companies to restore their interrupted ser- vices, but in all probability some days must elapse before the damages can be repaired. In the South of England snow again fell on Thursday morning. On Wednesday night, at a quarter past ten, a fire broke out at the Barkisland Mill, near Halifax, owned by the ex- ecutors of Mr: Ely Sutcliffe. Messrs. Bottomley Brothers, cotton spinners and doublers, also worked one portion of the mill. 'rho hands were at work in that portion worked by the owners, the firm having been working night and day for the last 12 months. A man named Robert Jagger, residing in Stainland, was burnt to death, and he leaves a wife and four children. Another man, named dward Clay, had his arm broken in two places, and one named George Howarth received a fracture of his jaw bone by jumping from the mill windows. The damage is roughly estimated at from £30,000 to £56,000, which is insured in the Liverpool, Lon- don, and Globe, and the Royal Insurance Companies. The fire originated through some portion of the machinery be- coming heated. A large number of hands are thrown out of employment, the building being entirely destroyed. An alarming accident has occurred on the North Staf- fordshire Railway. About eleven o'clock on Wednesday nights the last train from Stoke to Tunstall had arrived at what is called Longport Junction, when it was suddenly brought to a standstill, amidst the great consternation of the passengers, many of whom got out of the carriages, knee-deep in snow. On inquiries being snide, it was found that, owing to the heavy fall of snow, the line leading from Tunstall to Longport had been completely blocked by the running off the metals of two vans belonging to a goods train. The passengers' train was unable to pass, and was taken back to Burslem until about midnight, when a relief gang was sent for. The line, however, could not be cleared, and the Tunstall railway officials were telegraphed for. On their arrival, the whole of the passengers had to be directed across a viaduct by the aid of lamps, up to their knees in snow, and then taken fbrward by another train. Mr. Forster. on Thursday evening, addressed a crowded meeting of his constituent!! at Bradford, and entered into an elaborate defence of the Irish administration during the time that he held the office of Chief Seere'ery. He referred to the deplorable condition of Ireland at bile when he took office in I.Bto, and explained the circumstances under which the Government resolved not to ask Parliament to renew the Peace Preservation Act. Referring to the no-rent agitation, he paid the Land League and its leaders the oe:unpile-lent of saying that they forced the Govern- ment of the Queen into a hard struggle for supre- macy. Their weapons were not constitutional agi- tation, but words and acts which induced a state of terrorism throughout the country. It was the first agitation which he ever heard of the P.lF.in .strorth of which' wee to obtain its end not at the ballot box, no in Parliament, not by public opinion, but by terrorism to individuals. His 'resignation and_ thai cf arl Cowper were brought about by a difference with the other members of the Government—a difference, however, not in principle, but in matters of policy and of administration. He gave up the Chief Secre- taryship because he could not carry on the work under the conditions which were sought to be imposed upon him. When he left office crime and outrage bad largely diminished; the Land League had been suppressed as an open organisation; and there isottrA a brighter prospect for Ireland. It was with pleasure that be assisted his great chief the passing of the Land Aet, and especially in seeuraaag for the Irish tenants fixity of tenure. The right gentleman saw increasing signs of improve- ment IT:a. Ireland, and said he believed that the Government ~ad done, and was doing, what it could. Ghastly as the secret societies were, he had no doubt that the Government would get the better of them. THE ALHAMBRA THEATRE, LONDON BURNED, DOWN.— About one o'clock on Thursday morning the Alhambra Theatre, in Leicester Square, London, was discovered to be on fire, and information was at once despatched to the police and fire brigades in all the districts. Up to two o'clock it was impossible to get accurate information as to how the fire originated. The theatre had been closed as usual after the evening performance, and everything was left apparently safe. The first symptom of danger seems to have been ob- served about one o'clock on Thursday morning, and the alarm was at once sent in every direction. In an amazingly short space of time the building was full of flame, which burst through the windows and roof with incredible rapi- dity. The materials of the interior were well calculated to yield readily to the flames, and once they got hold of the roof the soft wind which.was blowing rapidly fanned them into a glowing furnace. A. strong force of police was soon in Leicester Square keeping back the public, who already began to crowd the thoroughfares leading to the place, from possible danger, and allowing the firemen room for their operations. Within half an hour the roof of the theatre I yielded to the flames which then burst up high into the air, followed by myriads of brilliant sparks, and accom- panied by volumes of grey smoke. The square was lighted up with a noonday brilliancy, and a ruddy glow was cast over the whole of the densely populated dis- trict of Soho. Thousands of people congregated from all parts, but they were kept far away from the burning building by strong cordons of police placed at the streets leading into Leicester-square. The greatest excitement pre- vailed in the locality, being one of the most densely popu- lated in the metropolis, and the streets very narrow. The Alhambra itself is flanked on each side by dwelling-houses, hotels, and schools, while behind it, extending from Cran- bonrne-street, down St. Martin's-lane are huge blocks of property used as dwelling-houses, and many of them let out in tenements. At one time it seemed as if the whole of the east side of Leicester-square would be destroyed, but the efforts of the well-disciplined fire brigade have been success- ful in limiting the flames to a space much less than could have been expected. The Alhambra itself is gutted and the building destroyed.

Mt:lmm IND ATTEMPTED StrlClDE.—EastFerry, a small village on the Trent side, about tern miles from Gains- borough, was on Wednesday the scene of a frightful murder and attempted suicide, the tragical ending of a police-court case heard at Gainsborougl. on the previous day. James Anderson, a farmer, had summoned and obtained a convic- tion against his son Charles, in whose favour James's wife had given evidence. During the cross-examination the wife of the prosecutor had complained of her husband's ill treat- ment, and declared she was afraid to live with him, and the son pleaded in extenuation of an admitted assault on his father that he had done it to protect his mother. The I Chairman of the Bench characterised it as the worst case of family dissension it had ever been his fortune to listen to, and intimated that only the plea of guilty induced the- magistrates to convict. . Having seen his convicted son bound over to keep the peace, Anderson returned to East Ferry', a village about a mile from his residence, and re- mained there all night. At noon on Wednesday he pro- ceeded to his own home, and found his wife alone. What passed is not known, but a short time afterwards the un- fortunate woman was discovered with her throat cut, the jugular vein severed, and quite dead. The murderer was found with his throat also cut, but not so seriously. In his hand was a pocket knife. It is supposed the unhappy pair qaarrelled, that the husband attacked the wife with his pocket knife, and after cutting her throat was induced by fear of the consequences to attempt his own life. .

RUNCORN SCHOOL BOARD. The Rev. Canon Barclay, chairman, presided over the monthly meeting held in the Board offices, Bridgewater- street, Runcorn, on Wednesday morning. There were also present the Rev. Father Fennelly, Messrs. John Simpson, T. Norman, J. Pritchard, P. Briscoe, R. Lea, and F. Rigby (clerk). THE WORKING ARRANGEMENTS OF THE BOARD. The first business-was the appointment of an assistant to the visitor.—Mr. SrupsoN said the arrangements of the Board were very different from those of any board of which he had -any knowledge. He found that it was customary for the clerk to do all the office work, and to take the prose- cutions. The clerk or assistants did a great portion of the work which the Runcorn Board's visitor did, and so far as his information went, the visitors did not do any office work at all. He could not tell which was the better arrangement, but he thought it would be well if they looked at the ques- tion before the appointment of assistant.—The CHAIRMAN: Bowyer distinctly stated that he had only one pair of legs. It was not so much a question of time as one of physique.— Mr. SIMPSON: But if the whole of the time of the visitor was given to the visiting, it would be such a very different thing from what it is now.—The CLERK said as a matter of fact the visitors at Widnes kept their own record. The routine of the Runcorn office was founded almost entirely upon the routine of the Liverpool School Board. The visitors' work was almost on all fours of routine of Liverpool, and in respect to the prosecutions of Liverpool, there was a head visitor who was responsible for all prosecutions.—Mr. SIMPSON remarked that from the reports of proceeding at Widnes, it appeared that the clerk always took the prosecutions, and the visitors' names never appeared at all.—The CLERK said the clerk to the Widnes Board gave his whale time to the work. And then the inspectors and visitors kept their own books.—Mr. PRITCHARD supposed that the visitors would have to give evidence against the delinquents at the police court. The proof would lay with the viaitors.—Mr. SIMPSON: With regard to office work, the visitors make their own records, but all calculations and posting taken from those records were done by the clerk or the assistants in the office.—The CLERK said the duty of the clerk in a place like Widnes was to direct the policy of the Board, to inspect and supervise all details.—Mr. Noneuer said be understood the visitort brought in their reports and filed them. Next morning they were entered up by the clerk's assistant. —The CLERK re- marked that years ago the officer at Liverpool was respon- sible for his own district and kept his own records. If that were not so he would not hare that special knowledge which was required when prosecutions-were made. It helped him immensely to keep his own reaord.—Mr. Suursaer said he was not saying that Widnes yr any other town's . arrangement was the best, but he understood that the arrange- ments in many boards were different from Runcorn, that he thought it would be well to understand the matter properly. —Mr. BOWYER, the officer, was called into the room, and ' in answer to questions, said he wet engaged three hours a day in office work. The recording ot his visiting occupied him about an hour a day. If he did not keep the books as he did he should be much wanting in evidence in conduct- ing prosecutions, and cases would fall through.—The CLERIC observed that it did not say that because other systems dif- fered from the system in use at Runcorn, that the latter was wrong.—Mr. Suersoet said certainly not, but the appoint- ment they were about to make gave rise to•much discussion timong the ratepayers with regard to the expense, and he thought it was well to discuss the matter for their satisfac- tion. (Hear, hear.)—Tbe CLERK: The way to keep down the expenses is to keep down the population. (Laughter.) If the population increased as it had done during the last emu years, year by year, it was obvious to any man who gave the subject the least reflection that there was one of two things—either Bowyer when appointed had work- com- mensurate with his salary or he had not enough to do when appointed. He (the clerk) knew that be had enough to do when appointed, and if he had enough to do seven years ago, it was obvious that he had more than enough to do now.—Mr. SIMPSON: I think Bowyer has enough to do.—The CLERK showed that since the Beard was formed 207 cases bad been taken under the bye-laws, 43 under the 11th section, and 25 under section 12. Only seven of these cases had been lost, and not because the Board failed to prove the cases, but "imply because the magistrates took a lenient view of them. (Hear, hear, and laughter.)—The CLERK said, with all humility, that it would not be a bad thing if other Boards were to see how Runcorn Board worked.—Mr. NORMAN: Yes, and learn from us.—Mr. SIMPSON said he had no change of system to recommend himself. NORMAN, seconded by Mr. LEA., it was resolved that the four first- named be requested to appear before the Board at their next meeting on the 10th January. VISITOR'S REPORT. In the returns for the past month, ending November 24th, you will notice that there is a decided improvement in the attendance at the various schools, as compared with the preceding month, the figures showing a total number on the rolls at the public elementary schools of 2,898, and an average attendance of 1898.6. These figures show an in- crease in the number on the rolls, as compared with the corresponding period of last year, of 139, and a decrease in the average attendance of 78-5. This decrease in the aver. age attendance is caused principally through the epidemic of scarlitina and measles, which have been so prevalent of late. lam however, glad to report that it has consider- ably abated', and that with the exception of Mill-brow and Pennington-row districts the town is comparatively free, but there are still a many children, especially the infants, unable to attend from the effects of the epidemic, who have not yet got sufficiently strong to attend school regularly. The number in attendance at private adventure schools under 9d per week, for the month ending November 24th, was 71. During the past month I have served 27 notices on parents whose children have been attending school irregularly, there having been no sufficient reason given for their non-attendance. This was all the business of public interest.

The Daily Nctrs correspondent at Rangoon telegraphs:— The eldest son of the late King of Burmah has escaped-I from Benares. The Foreign Department is unable to trace him. It is believed that he is on bis way to Upper Bnrmah to raise a rebellion. There is great excitement in Rangoon.
ENGLISH RAILWAYS AND FOREIGN STOCKS.
EPORT OF THE MONTH.

IIHE apprehension of an imminent demand of gold for New York and the continuous flatness of the Paris Bourn have paralysed our markets during the past month. Quotations t moved spasmodically, fluctuating from day to day according as purchases or sales predominated. In fact, business has of late been so contracted, especially in the Foreign market, that the purchase or sale of £50,000 stock has been sufficient to affect quotations sensitively. The persistent selling on Wench ac- count created considerable uneasiness, as it was currently be- lieved that it was owing to the precarious pAtion of seme of the most respectable financial institutions in France. The real fact is that the late fall in Paris was principally due to market manipulations on the part of the haute fieance in Trance with a view of bringing about the resignation of the present Finances Minister and the reappointment of M. L6an Say; the sales were mainly confleed to 5 per cent. Rentes and Ottoman Banks, as has bees shown by the extraordinarily low continua- tion rates at the last settlement of the Paris Bourse. As soon se the markets react these two stocks will be prominent in recover- ing former prices. The fall in Imperial Ottoman Banks commenced on the ap- pearance of a quasi-protest on th 3 part of a leading firm against the reeoeniti ni of the new Turkish Loan by the Com- mittee of the Stock Exchange. We do not believe that this loan has attracted English investors, and even in Paris its suc- cess ie very doubtful. The revenues professedly hypothecated to subscribers of the earlier loans. What reliance can there he felt that at a future and no distant period the Sultan will not _ borrow from the Galata bankers on these Identical 'venues?

EGYPTIAN STOCKS have been depressed owing to French selling. Wild and ridiculous rumours were in- dustriously circulated by those interested in the general tall, that holders of these Stocks began to lose confidence at the very time when everything tends to inspire more confiden"e in therm than in any other foreign stock. But it is by no means an un- usual phenomenon in matters of finance to see a stock depressed and absolutely neglected on the eve of a great rise. To thoso 'who are independent of market influences there are no other senrities which can be recommended with greater contideua than Egyptian Stocks. We are credibly informed that Ilse question of the rearrangement of the Egyptian Debt is now under the consideration of the o,..binet, and the Government actuaries have already reported favourably on a scheme which, while possibly diminishing tbe interest, will give the bon& holders such additional compensation and safeguards as to amount to an English guarantee. This will be amomnanied by a scheme for the rapid amortisatiun of the United Stock at par._

OME RAILWAYS.—As usual at this period of the ee_ year there has been a great contraction of business, and prices have ass rule tended downwards. The fall has bean most marked in Sheffield "A," North-Eastern, Brighten "A" and Dover" A." The two former have been influenced by the reduction in the price of iron, consequent on the suspensionof railway construction in America. As the general businesseE these lines, apart from iron, shew signs of great expansion,ves regard the depression as temporary, and look for latgelyire- creased business and much higher prices with the turn of the year. The traffic returns of other heavy lines still show that the general trade of the country is displaying material progress, and though prices are at a comparatively high level, there is little to discourage the investor. The small amouut of the Great Western Ordinary Stock influences many buyers, and in spite of the recent unfavourable weather' accompanied by 'severe floods in the West of Ergland, the traffics show suck vitality that Tr e are inclined to select this stock as by far the best for both investment and speculation. The rapid extension of the Bristol and Milford Haven Dock systems is leading to the rapid development of trade with both Americas, and before many years the Ordinary Stock of this line will be quote I even higher than London and North-Western. The passenger lines still show disappointing results, the earnings of the Brighton line being especially bad. At one time Brighton " A's" • receded to West on the public advertisement of thee proposed line from Beckenham to Eastbourne. We alluded So this project in our last Monthly Report, and it is sale clent to add that it. has the support of the Duke of Devonshire and other large landholders along the proposed route. There are other causes of gerat diseouragem nt, notably t e large increase of fixed' charges, the adSitional workieg expense, the suspension of building operations at Brighton, which have hitherto bent a source 01 much revenue to the comp-nv, and the get dua:le augmtnting prices oi labour and mateTials„ Is seems improbable that the dividend wit elec.(' 3 per cent. an the "A's," nor is the prospect for the new half-yesr much mo eecouraging. We are eout to coati are wish a period when the company earned an increase of about a 40,000, and it is very unlikely that trafti e Will show much augmeetation. Fixed. ehargts will continue to !ncrease rapidly tor the next two yea-s, and the vast additional rolling et ck paid for Ourieg the lest. four years at the expense of NITA al will soon largely add to the lee mnotive e,penses nail; comes into the repairing sheds. Should the Midland Reilway decide on extending s ,ut hwards to Ettore-- ham and Brighton, the future of the Brighton Oompany will be indeed glo any, and it seems ce-tain that only a large reduction in fares and additional facilities to the travellieg public will avoid competition from either the 3f.ilprid or an independent line. Had it not been that an exegete-a ed "bear" aczount has been for some time in existence, the A stock would probably have receded to par. T e recent rapid os'illation upwards .has been solely due to a fright en the part, of speculators for the fall, due to rumours that promineut officials of the fhiehton line had again comasence • operations fe• the rise. The Greek Eilyn irate is repor eel to be eV 1 in existence, als hough the losses sustained must now be immense.

AMERICAN STOCKS have been no exception to the general fiatne.ss, the temporary stringency in New York being sufficient to counteract the magnificent traffic returns of all the leading lines. Delayers and Wabash have suffered most in price, rumours that the mortgage interest on these railways would not be paid being industriously circulated by the bears: Our November report pointed out that the constructors of the enormous additional mi,eage built during the last three years are still embarrassed by the lock up of their capital, and the knowledge of this fact deters investors from taking advantage of the present low level of prices. Much ignorant nomeuse has been talked of the war of rates in the North West, but the points_ in dispute ate comparatively insignificant, and it is prob..ble that before these lines are in prints, means of arrange meat will have been found. The railway presidents met on Saturday last, and considerable progress was made in the de- tails of settlement. There has been very good buyine of the First Mortgage B.inds of the New York, Pennsylvania, and Ohio Railway, the net earnings of which show an enormous advance. The forthcoming dividend, parrly pay.ble in scrip. readily saleable at about 50 per cent., will be equal to about percent, equal at the present price to 9 per cent. per annum. It is notorious that Jay Gould is endeavouring to tviquire this line as a link in his proposed new route from the South West to New Y,rk.- We still confidently suggest New York Central, Illinois, and PennrylvanTas as thoroughly sound and rapidly impmving trierns.

teIANA.DIAN RAILWAYS have displayed great steadine6ll A../ In spite of the downward tendency of the American mar- ket. with which department prices usually move sympatheti- cally. The Trunk traffics are simply phenomenal, azd the receat declaration of the dividend of the Grand Trunk Second Prefer- ence in full is eminently reassuring. This stock, with nearly 5 per cent accrued dividend, is rediculously cheap, and at 104 should amply repay an investor. It is expected that the late traffic will close abut December th, and the closing will be followed by an increase in the East-bsund rates. Tile war of rates among the GrariVr lirvs has caused an immen,e accurnu- lat Lin of grain at Chicago, Which is now being rapidly sent for- ward to the Atlantic sea.blard.

ber for the University of Cambridge, is a gentleman who by his dos,. connection with the late Government may f,,e fairly looked upon as a not irresponsible politician. On Wednesday evening, Mr. RAI/OS spoke at. Heywood in support of the cancNature of Mr. W. W. B. HULTON, one of the Cc,`nserva- tive candidates for the representation of sOuth- east Lancashire, and we venture to think t:?1/4at some of his statements are rather extra- ordinary. lir. RAIKES of course, is not, and would not be, a member of the Liberal Cabinet, thongh it is just possible that some day he may join the Tory magic circle, yet singularly enough he is able to inform us that there are two parties in the Cabinet, one of which on the' one day is uppermost, and on another the other. Even assuming that this description of the Cabinet is correct, which we very much dispute, how, we should like to know, does Mr. RAIKES comb by his informa- tion? No member of the Cabinet would be likely to make him a confidant, but even if he were a confidant 'and had some such informa- tion as that he gave expression to conveyed to him, he would be acting in a most ungentlemanly and mischievous manner in betraying the trust. But the stop, carries its own refutation with it. No Cabinet could exist many days in which there were two contending parties, and in the case of the present Cabinet there does not seem to be the slightest evidence of any disagreement. The whole story is a wicked, invention of Mr RAIKES in order to make political capital, but it is scarcely likely to find much credence beyond the very limited audience to whom it was addressed, if indeed it is believed even by his hearers. Mr RAIKES finds fault with the Irish policy of Liberal Governments. He condemns the disestablishment of the Irish Church ; and traces all the ills to which Ireland is heir to the carrying out of that Measure Further, he laments that after Lord BEACONSFIELD had been six years in power, and 'ld not attempt to do anything for Ireland, Mr: GLADSTONE should have passed such a measure of justice as the Irish Land Act. Mr. RAIKES is one of the very few men who dare now to assert that the disestablish- ment of the Irish Church has not been pro- ductive of a great amount of good to Ireland; and the benefits which that most equitable measure confers will be felt, we believe., still more in the future than they have been in the past. It is all very well for Mr. KAIKES to talk about the confiscation of Irish land by the Act passed during- the present Parliament, but had such-a measure not been necessary, it would never have received the assent of the two Houses of Parliament by so large majorities. Surely Mr. RAIKES has forgotten that at the time that measure was passed Ireland was suffering from something worse than "pestilence and famine," to use the words of Lord BEACONSTIELD ; or has he forgotton that the very last measure the Arrears Act Lord SALISBURY threatened to throw out of the House of Lords altogether, or rather to so mutilate it That it would have been of no effect, yet when the crucial time came he had to abandon his intention for the very reason that he ,knew he would not be supported. Parliament is not in the habit of passing measures of confisca- tion. Mr. RAIKES. WO, Complains that on the question of education the Liberal party had not only aimed at compilsory education, but at the teaching in elementary schools of no defined form of Christian religion. The religious question is an old bogy, and it ill becomes Mr. RAIKES to revive it. The Liberal party, as Mr. RAIKES knows, are as anxious as the Tory party is ever likely to be for the religious as well as the secular educa- tion of the young, and they believe the Sunday school to be the place in which religious dogma ought to be imparted; but they do object, and very properly, too, to dogmatism in the day school, which ought to be re- served for secular educatioh only. Mr. RAIKID3, in our opinion, is not very happy in his reference to the Egyptian question. He does not speak the truth N),f_en he says our policy has been one of "contemptuous defiance of the SULTAN of Turkey," in whose goodwill, he adds, it is most important for us to reckon. Mr. RAIKES had better consult his blue-books before he again speals on this subject. To our mind, we paid far too much deference to the SULTAN of Turkey. Turkey was implored and entreated to do the work which it ought legitimately to have done, but Turkey dallied and did not do it, in conse- quence of which the -restoration of order in Egypt became more difficult, and it was not indeed until the very last moment—and when she found she could do no other—that England interfered. A great deal too much consideration has been shown for Turkey. But apart from that altogether we contend that if there is one thing more than another which the present Government has done to well establish their reputation in the confi- dence of the people of this country it is the way, in which they carried through the Egyptian war. Nobody knows that better than the Tories themselves, many of them have from time to time very generously actnowledged it in their public meetings, and it seems to have been reserved for Mr. RAIK.ES only to detract from the Government in this regard. Speeches such as the one under considera- tion are not calculated to do the Conserva- tive party any permanent good. If they are of any benefit whatever it must be transient. They are altogether too flippant and too much devoid of facts to commend them to an intelligent and discriminating public, and coming from a gentleman in Mr. RAIKES' position they must have their effect in damaging him considerably in the public estimation. Cambridge University has indeed very little cause to be proud of its member.

TILE ALLEGED EmBEEELENTPNT BY A PAWNDEORICE'S MANAGER AT RIINCORIL-At the Runcorn Police Court, on Tuesday, befere Messrs. W. Ranks and Henry Reynolds, Thomas Hicks was brought up on remand, charged with stealing is., the property of Horatio Syred, on the 27th. From the evidence of Mr. Syred it appeared that be kept a clothier's shop in Chnrch-street, of which the prisoner had been the manager for five or six weeks. On the 27th Nov., in consequence of suspicions he bad respecting the prisoner, he came to Runcorn, and marked a number of coins. amongst others the shilling produced. He handed the money to his wife, who sent the servant from Liverpool to the shop to make some purchases. She expended 245., and amongst the money she gave the prisoner was the marked shilling. Shortly afterwards Inspector Hollingworth went to the shop and searched the prisoner, upon whom he found the marked shilling. In the prosecutor's books the prisoner appeared to have accounted for 235. 6d. of the 245. The prisoner elected to be summarily dealt with, and, in defecce, said it was part of his arrangement with Mr. Syred that he should provide coals for the house. He admitted taking the shilling, but it was for the . purpose of buying coal of which they had none.—The Bench be- lieved the statement, and discharged the prisoner.—Hicks and W. Hutchinson were then charged with stealing a serge jacket, the property of Horatio Syred.—The evidence of In- spector Hollingworth showed that when he went to the prose- cutor's shop, he diecovered that Hutchinson had been living in the kitchen, where he found the serge jacket, which was similar to others in the shop. It had apparently been worn by some person, but as there was nothing further than that fact to connect the prisoners with the case, they were dis- oharged.—A charge of embezzlement had been preferred against Hicks, butowiog to the unsatisfactory way in which the bobks had been kept, it was impossible to prove any specific charge against him, and th.a Mt: was nut prooeeded ' _ with.

HOW TO MITE 1 CHRISTMAS PODDING. —Take three - quarter's of a pound of flour, a large teaspoonful of Borwick's Gold Medal Baking Powder, two ounces of bread crumbs, a pound and a half of suet, two porencls of raisins one pound of currants, ten ounces of sugar, two ounces of almonds, one pound of mixed candied peel, salt and spice to taste, mix ingredients well together arid add six eggs well beaten, half- a-pint of old ale and one quartern of brandy. Both civil and criminal business will he taken at these assizes, which are expected to commence, as usual, about the 11th of January next. A Row a:r WIEKES CENTRAL STATION.—At Widnes Petty Sessions, on Monday, Michael Dafferv, Patrick Der- yin, and John Dempsey, were charged with being drunk and disorderly, at the Central Station, Widnes, on the previous i day, and also with wilfully damaging the booking office door. On Sunday afternoon the prisoners entered the booking office and asked for tickets by the 3-35 train to Warrington. Mr. Joseph Balshew, the booking clerk, saw the condition, and reftesed to comply with their request, at the same time ordering them to leave the station. They refused, and commenced to quarrel amongst themselves. During thelr struggle they fell against the door of the booking office, and broke it. Thomas Davies and Emmanuel Fox, porter and signalman respectively, at- tempted to restrain the prisoners, but without avail, and Fox was roughly handled by them.—The prisoners alleged that the breaking of the door was an accident, and denied that they assaulted the officials. They were, however, fined 103. and costs each for being drunk, a similar amount for the damage which they were ordered to pay for, the total amount in each case amounting to 355. LoolL BANKRUPTS, &c. EXTRAOBDrNART CELITtGB AASLIZ/LT AGAINST I SON AT RuNCORN.—On Monday, at Runeorn Petty Sessions, Robert Moores, a strong4ooking fellow, was brought up on remand, charged with haying on the 27th ult. assaulted his mother, Eleanor Moores, who appeared in court with her face very much discoloured and bruised.—Prisoner pleaded not ,guilty.—The prosecutrix said her son got married on Sun- day, and at 20 minutes past 10 on Monday morning she thought she would go to hint and enjoy herself. She went into "Walker's," where her son and several others were, and called for four "whiskies." The defendant also called for one. After the liquor had been drunk, the defendant and his companions left the house, and she followed, when the de- fendant "up with his fist" and knocked her to the ground. The condition in which she was now was the result of his ill-usage. None of the witnesses who saw the occurrence dare give evidence, because the defendant was such a "treacherous lad." He had assaulted her scores of times previously, and she had frequently made complainte to Supt. Williamson.—Prosecutrix called James Yates, living in Millbrow, who said he was in the "Long Pull" with the defendant when his mother entered. She said "I have copt you, have I," at the same time seizing the defendant's glass of whiskey, and drank half of it. Then she gave him a "smack in the face," saying "we will be comfortable to- day." She began to use very offensive and obscene lan- guage, in consequence of which the barman gave her a glass containing tea and milk, and told her to "rinse her mouth out." The defendant and the other persons left the prosecutrix in the house, and shortly afterwards they were told she had fallen in the street. He (witness) went to her, and dragged her to the Red Lion in Greenway-road, when in conscAnence of her conduct he went from her. Subsequently he went to her again and took her home.--The defendan.lt made a somewhat similar statement, and Mrs. Jane Ly(Uate, of 41 Regent- street, deposed to seeing the prosecutrix fall from the steps of the "Long Full" into the roaa, , thereby bruising her L face in the manner in which it was. HELE7.R.-011 Monaay evening the annual ball in connection with the St. Helens Conservative Club was held in the Assembly Room, Town Hall. There were a large number of ladieeeand gentlemen present. The masters of the ceremonies were Major Win- dus, and Messrs. J. J. Tickle, J.K. Bicball, and Critchlev, and the stewards Messrs. J. Massey, R: Lawton, F. Farana, C. Culshaw, and H. Swift. BTIRGLA.E.S WA.RRINGTON.—No fewer than three lock-up shops in one of the principal streets el the town were entered by burglars early on Saturday morning last. The premises entered were those occupied by Messrs. Gar- nett and Sons, Mr. S. Moss, and Messrs. G. and W. Fell, all situate in Sankey-street, and were broken into from the - roofs and syklights. • Drawers were forced open, but the burglars obtained very little for their pains, all they secured being coppers and stamps to the value of 3s. or 4e. The • police have issued a notice stating that a gang of expert • burglars and housebreakers have commenced operations in the town, and cautioning tradespeople and others not to leave cash, valuables, stamps, ate., in lock-up premises. BILLIARD MATc-n: BENzarr v. Moncux.—A rare treat for lovers of the vane of billiards was provided by Mr. William Melling, of the New Market Hotel, Earlestown, on Thursday evening last. It consisted in an "exhibition" match at billiards,between Alfred Bennett champion player of the Midlands, and A. W. Morgan, of Manchester, the latter receiving 150 start in 1.000, the game taking place on the capital table owned by Mr. Melling. There was a fair attendance of gentlemen interested in the game up to n point when it became evident that Bennett (who was in splendid form) would run out the winner by a great number of points. In the result, the total score of Bennett was 1,000, Morgan 522. The game commenced about seven o'clock, and occupied about two hours and a half. COLLIERY ACCIDENT AT TRAIT° HEATH.:—On Wednes- - day an inquest was held at Thatto Heath, before Mr. Hardy, deputy coroner, touching the death of James Pickavance, a collier, 24 years of age. It appeared that the deceased was a browman at Sherdley collieries, belong- ing to Messrs. Bourses and Robinson, and that on the let I inst. he had been descending a shaft in a two-decked cage, when the lower deck caught the side of the shaft and the deceased's leg was caught between the cage and the side of the pit. His leg was so seriously hurt that it had to he amputated, notwithstanding which, however, deceased succumbed to his injuries on the following day. A verdict of accidental death was returned. Moxon, McKinley, Pezmington, Lewis, and Slater; Mr. Brewis (clerk), and Mr. Knighton (deputy clerk).—Mr. Brewis stated that be had sent a letter of con- dolence to the relatives ot the late Mr. James Woodward, who was a member of the Board, in acknowledgment of which a letter had been received from Mr. T. Cook thanking the Board en behalf of the relatives. Mr. Brewis also inti- mated that Mr. P. McKinley had been eiected to the vacant place on the Board, at a vestry meeting held on the 20th November.—The registrar's (Mr. Grant) returns showed that £35 Os. V. had been received during the present month. There had been 79 burials, and the balance in hand was £9 15s. pd.—This was all the business of public interest before the Board. TILE "SMALL GANG " AT WORK IN TIER John Murray Murray (10), who had been previously before the court, Thomas Garrity (17), 1, Ship-yard, and Michael Calligan (17), 16, Dolman's-lane, were charged, at Warring- ton Police Court, on Monday, with stealing two pocket knives, value is. 41., the property of William Horrocks, in the Fair Ground, on Saturday night.—The prisoner, a general dealer from Manchester, bad a seen in the Fair Ground, and left it for a few minutes in charge of a youth named Peter Clare. About nine e'clocic, the three prisoners went to the stall, and Murray by way of ruse said "I want a light," he having a pipe or cigar in his hand. In getting the light Murray laid hold of a stick and Carr told him to put it down, but the prisoners began to push him about. He, however, saw Murray and Callaghan take knives, and when the prosecutor came he told him of the robbery. Carr then went to the police station where he identified Murray, who had been locked up on another charge, and the other prisoners were arrested on Sunday.—The Chief Constable said Callagban had only just left a reformatory school, where he had been for four years. He, however, had joined the gang again. They were called the "small gang," and they did just what they liked.—Garrity's father said his son did everything but what he told him.--Murrav and Garrity were each committed for three months hard. labour, and Callaghan for one month. FATAL FILL DOW:MT-AIRS AT WABEINGT3T. Barker. (deputy coroner) held an inquest on Tuesday, at the General Wolfe Inn, Church-street, Warrington, touching the death of a woman named Ann Mackay, of Jackson's- yard, Church-street. From the evidence adduced it would • I appear that on the previous Tuesday the deceased, who had had some drink, went to bed with the rest of the household, at the usual time: About three o'clock on the following morning the deceased's son, a young man named William Briggs, was awakened by hearing moans, and he called a lodger named Sykes, who went downstairs and found the • deceased lying at the bottom of the steps- with her bead downwards, and her legs on the stairs. Sykes told Briggs t hat his mother bad fallen downstairs, and with his assist- ance he carried her to bed. Owing to the deceased having been under the influence of drink nothing was thought of. the occurrence until about seven o'clock. in the morning, when it was noticed that deceased was moaning. Dr. Fox . was then called in, and he gave it as his opinion that the spinal cord was injured, and it was impossible for the de-. ceased to get better. The deceased expired on Saturday about six o'clock. She bad been in the habit of going downstairs for a drink of water or cold tea when she had had drink, and it is supposed she got up for this purpose. and fell downstairs. The jury returned a 'verdict of "Acci- dental death." A BARIUM'S GRUNAIWES.—i ease was heard before.

It was a claim by Julian Donnolley, a barmaid, against Samuel Walker, who keeps a publichouse near the _Market Hall, for wages which plaintiff held to be due. Mr. Swift appeared for the plaintiff, and Mr. Riley for the defendant.— Mr. Swift said the plaintiff had been a barmaid in the employ of the defendant, and brought that case to recover three weeks wages and one month's wages- in lieu of a proper notice. The whole question would depend on whether his honour thought the plaintiff's dismissal, which was an Instant dismissal, was justifable. The plaintiff was.in the employ of the defendant for three weeks up to the 10th. November, and she was engaged as usual at her work on that day when the*fendant and his daughter, he believed she. was, came into the room and ordered her to leave at once. Miss Walker accused her of being drunk, the defendant also. saying the same. He, however, should call witnesses to show. that she had not been drunk. The slim of 163 101 had been paid into court, he added, to cover the three weeks wages,, so that bnly the question of the justifiableness or otherwise of the dismissal remained to be decided.—The plaintiff was then called, and stated that she had been engaged at £l6 per year, and it was agreed that a month's notice on either side should terminate the engagement. After being told to leave the house she went into her own bedroom and bolted_ the door. Whilst there Miss Walker came to the door, and on plaintiff refusing to admit her until she wasalressal. Miss Walker broke open the door, and plaintiff then saw two policemen standing. Miss Walker then agai ordered her sway, and plaintiff shortly after' went down into the bar to get her scissors and thimble, where Miss Walker introduced to her a gentleman who she said was her solicitor, but who, it afterwardaturned out, was, no solicitor, but a Mr. Goldsmith. .5-be (Plaintiff) said "Good morning" to him, and he replieJ, "Yoe bad bette? take your wages, my dear girl," but sho refused to have the. 15s. offered to her by Miss Walker. Since that day she had. frequently applied for other situstaans, bat had failed to, get them, owing to tb-a defendant's not giving her a go?d, character. -—-- - - - OPING THE WRONG GRAVE. air,—Will you please give space to the following in your wide-spread journal :—Having followed the remains of a beloved and respected friend, to the cemetery, on Sunday last, and after the usual ceremony in the mortuary, it was discovered, to the utter dismay of the relatives and friends of the departed, that the wrong grave had been opened. A mistake had been made no doubt, and a very serious one under the circumstances, inasmuch as we had to stand in the coldand rain until the proper grave (after several slips) was opened, during which progress, it was suggested by one of the officials that the corpse be lowered into the unfinished grave, the minister to perform the remaining portion of the ceremony, and the friends of the above to retire, after which they would exhume the remains, and finish the grave, and again bury the dead. To my mind, Mr. Editor, the above 'suggestion was unfortunate ene, it added insult to injury, and called forth a speech from a lady, I believe a sister of deceased, who observed "If that is the way they did their businesss in Warrington, it showed they were uncivilised." an expression coincided with by many present. After the above facts, to say nothing of the feelings of friends, I think, Mr. Editor, something ought to be done to prevent the recurrence of such not very decent and unseemly pro- ceedings in future. Apologising for this liberty, I beg to remain, &c., &c., A FOLLOWER. Warrington, December sth, 1882.
THE BRITISH WORKMAN PUBLIC HOUSE Co., LIMITED: A CHALLENGE.

Sir,—The statements contained in the communicated paragraph inset ted in your last issue as a report of the pro- ceedings at the annual general meeting of this company held last week, demand a reply from me. That reply they shall have, and if, after a perusal of this letter and any answer to it that may be forthcoming, there remains in any fair and unbiased mind the shadow of a doubt as to where the truth is, it shall not be from any ambiguity on my part. The chairman, " Thomf-s Morris, Esq.," is reportsd to have said that " Libra "had "assumed a great deal which was en- tirely without facts to support it, and if he had before writing to the public Precs only taken the trouble to have privately enquired from himself he would have furnished him with every information, as they as a company had nothing to conceal." In reply to these remarks, I have to say, first, that every figure I have given, and every statement I have made is absolutely taken from or based upon the printed accounts and report signed by" Thomas Morris" and "Hentyßoberts," or upon speeches made by the same parties at the opening of the Milner-street new house on the 23rd ultimo, and I challenge anyone to show the contrary. Of course, if these gentlemen have appended their names to accounts and reports, or have made statements in speeches which are incor- rect, the responsibility is not mine. Second: I did not consult Mr. Morris before writing to the public Press because upon such questions as those at ibsue he is not erectly the man I should think of going to, and in justification of this view I need only repeat a couple of sentences t oat his speech of the 23rd ult., as reported in your issue of the 25th. He said: " Their critic (that is • Libta 7) thought they should not pay any dividend until they lead wiped off their depre- ciation account. That was to say, they had spent .E4OO over and above their capital, £230 of which they bad paid off; hut this 'gentleman thought they shouM pay it all before they declared a dividend, or even paid their servants properly."' A man who muddles up two essentially distinct and different questions in this fashion—apparently con- founding the duty of causing the nominal book value of the fixed plant or property of a concern to represent its fair and reasonable or market value by a wear and tear or depreciation charge against revenue, with the act of increasing the capital liability until the total sum of such capital liability

reaches the amount of the gross capital expenditure (whether the amount of that expenditure represents actual value or not), and thinks that to adopt the latter course is to dispose, at the same time, of the question of depreciation —is, to my mind, anything but a safe financial guide. Third: Mr. Morris is so very ready to charge me with "assuming a great deal without facts to support it," and so backward at coming forward with a single instance in which I was wrong (notwithstanding his two attempted replies), that I now ask him to tqll me when and where, and in what words, I ever stated that before they "even paid their servants properly" they should equalise the amount of their capital liabilities with that of the nominal value of their fixed assets. I have never alluded in any way to the pay of their servants, and I must ask Mr. Morris to sub- stantiate or wandraw his charge. Had it not been for the fulsome flattery of the report you insert with respect to the performance of the seuetary at the annual meeting of the shareholders I should have guessed that Mr. Roberts himself was its author. He is re- ported to have," in a lengthy statement, showed conclusively that the concern was prospering in a most satisfactory degree, and that instead of their affairs being as Libra' would have them believe, the exac;; opposite was the case.'' This is a very eerious indictment, and fairly takes away my breath. So, before tackling Mr. Roberts, I will rest for a few seconds, and whilst so resting I may remark upon the ominous omission of this ve,y clever gen- tleman to give a single instance or proof of any erroneous statement on my part, and this notwithstanding that I haVe invariably given chapter and vette for eeery charge pre- ferred and exception taken, in respect of his company's affairs. InsteAd of following my example, in their allega. tions against me both he and the cuairman, in spite of the latter boast that" they had nothirg • conceal," have very carefully conceated the bases (that is fir:7 have any) of their answers to me, and have very carefully abstained temn entering into detail or rnak;ng a single gno'n.tion from my letters. Th ,7; not stated a single perticular wherein what I have urged has been in the least degree inaccurate, let alone the opposite the clue state of the case. Having new -had time to recover from the effect upon my nervous system of the eecretaiy's " le.tehander " I procerd to examine it. "He showed conclusively that instead of their affairs being as 'Libra' would have them believe, the exact opposite was the ca..e." Sir, I doubt that he show anything of the kind; indeed, I deny that could or can do it. What were my cha.rgcl? I IN:11 reP• oitulate them. They were, that whereas the print Id report elt 1 that the shareholders were call:1 together (among other things) to cmider the balance sheet of the company, that no balance

sheet was given ; that the important- items of the banker's and cash balances were not given in any account, or even referred to; that the accounts given were all of them incor- rectly stated; that the profit and los account was made up in the form of a cash account (?); that the dividend account was debited with what it should be credited with, and vice versa; that the capital account was debited instead of being credited with the contributions of the stareholders, and that into it were in' •oduced items which had nothing in the world to do with "capital," as understood by commercial authorities; and lastly, that since the formation of the com- pany not a farthing had ever been charged against revenue for "wear and tear" on the property of the company, a .class of property peculiarly liable to rapid depreciation. These, sir, are my statements concerning the accounts and ,position of Mr. Robe.}s' company, aid to them I "pin my 1 .colours." I challenge Mr. Plberts, Mr. Morris, Mr. Coun- cillor Francomb, or Mr. William Long to show in what , particular I am wrong. Nay, I go further, and hereby undertake that if one, any, or all of them combined, will prove that I have made a single statement which cannot be fairly based upon the report and accounts to which the names of "Thomas Mortis" and "Henry' Roberts" are attached or on speeches made by these individuals, I will Immediately hand over £lO to the treasurer of the War- rington Infirmary. But there must 12 no shuffling. The charges must be " ainarely "met. So f..r, the only item in pay list of !staietures, to which a reply has been attempted, as that with respect to dep-eciation. On this queltion I shall not allow the shareholders to be baml3ozled and per- suaded that" they can eat their cake and Yet have it " if I can help it. In the last printed report it is distinctly stated that £.219 163. 4d. of the undivided profits with- held from the shareholders up to the end of their wear just • closed, is" to be applied to the !eduction of the debt on capital," and that by thus capitalising profit to this extent the directors get rid "of the necessity for increasing the share capital of the company by this sum." This means that having spent £1,222 on property .and having only £798 in share capital, they have extra capital to obtain from somewhere; that they have got £219 on account of same, and that they have got this not by becoming liable for 219 new shares, but by becoming liable for £219, which they have withheld from the existing shareholders. In other words, the directors have increased the company's rainy liability by £219 —it does not matter whether it has been got from old shareholders or by the issue of new shares and to this in itself there can be no objection. But to do this and then to say, as Mr.. Morris does, that by doing so they also meet the question of depreciation is sheer nonsense. To increase your capital liability to your old or to new shareholders, or to ether outsiders, does not add a penny to the value of your alsets, or make up for the diminished value of your pro- perty. In the case of this £219, the money has actually been spent, and is included in the item of £1,222, and the question remains : Why have the directors of this concern allowed five or six years to elapse without charging aity.
