Sir,—Perhaps the following facts and jottings will interest "Newtonian," and other of your readers :—ln ShwayYoe's "The Burman: his Life and Notions," it is recorded that among desirable " transincorporations " are included the white elephant, the hare, and pigeon-. But the Burman despises the ant for the reason that. "like the maggot and earthworm, it lives on excrements and all manner of filth." I hope my recording this fact will not vex the soul of "Newtonian." Another curious fact in connection with entomology is the rigid observance the Burman pays to the first of the five rules," Thou a-thet go ma that hnin," "Thou shalt not take any life at all." Hardened convicts will not even harm the vermin that infest their mattresses. Now I think this is carrying the interpretation of the spirit of "" the first five rules" too far. I fancy that here in England, so-called vegetarians would not hesitate to kill fleas, not- withstanding their professed objection to countenance the slaughter of warm-blooded and cold-blooded animals. "Newtonian" will be glad to hear that bees are held in higher estimation than ants. The honey is used to embalm bodies before burial, and is afterwards sold in the bazaars. That is the reason Englishmen fight shy of it. What is termed "tapping the governor" does not commend itself to delicate palates. But to get back to the hare. A favourite myth with Buddhists is that of the hare Kalpas, since it is believed by them that the Lord of Truth appeared on earth in the form of that animal. "All creatures were making offerings to the Buddha' who was then engaged in preaching the sacred law. The hare bethought himself that he too must give some alms. Bat what had he to give? Man might bring costly gifts; the lion found it easy to offer the tender flesh of the fawn; birds of prey brought dainty morsels; fish could produce no less tasty signs of devotion; even the ant was able to drag along grains of sugar and aromatic leaves; but the hare, what had he? He might gather the most tender succulent shoots from the sunny forest glades, but they were useless even to form a *ouch for the Great Teacher. There was nothing but his own body, and that he freely offered. The Supreme Lord declined the sacrifice, but in remembrance of the pious in- tention, placed the figure of the hare in the moon, and there it remains as a symbol of the queen of the night to the present day. This confirms the legend howked out by those youngsters, and alluded to in a previous letter. I have alluded to the male domestic fowl bird in a previous letter, and perhaps the following will interest pitmen and ethers who indulge in "illegitimate sport" when they get an opprtunity A little below Mandalay, on the river, near the Ava road, there is a huge castellated pagoda, the Shway Gyet-yet, raised in commemoration of another per., formance of the Budh, in an avator countless ages ago. The tale is that "in a season of grievous dearth, when all flesh was dying of famine, the Great Master, then in the shape of a jungle-fowl, spied a holy pilgrim in the last extremity of want. There was none to pity him, none to save him from death; and the Budh, conquering even in that distant time one of the latest lost of the ten deadly sins—the love of life—surrendered himself to save another. Hence the pagoda standing out boldly on a great rock over the river. To the east is a representation of a fowl in stone recalling the event; and before this, daily by the pagoda slaves and others, and on feast days by hundreds of worshippers, plentiful heaps of gilded grains are strewn." What a simple and eloquent sermon. And we speak of these people as idolators and heathens! And now, before I attempt to" make even" with "Newtonian" in the matter of tails, allow me to congratulate hirq on his success in repairing the incubating apparatus with a view to his logical or metaphorical nightingale again bursting into prose or song. He has evidently been more successful as an amateur tinker than I was as an amateur chimney-sweep. He credits me with want of patience, but see what persever- auce, added to the "waiting virtue," has done in his case an 4 in mine. Here is Shway Yoe's account of the Burmese eats :—" The harmless, necessary cat is not abundant. There are, however, few villages without one or two of them. What becomes of the kittens is a mystery. Perhaps they go wild and take to the woods. Perhaps the pariah dog eats them when their mother is out foraging. At any rate, the fact remains that they increase but very slowly. The Bur- man cat is more fortunate than his Malay congener in pos- sessing a tail, but asserts relationship with that animal in the r-ssession of a horny hook, with this difference that the har4 excrescence is at the end of a tail of fair dimen- sions instead of being humbly situated on the rump, as is the case with the Straits tabby." I should like to know if it is owing to the absence of this hook from the tails of our cats that they steal fish from our larders instead of catching it in the rivers and ponds? But I had perhaps better treat this subject with caution, bearing in mind the Lancashire adage that those who play with cats come to grief. I cannot just now spare time to follow " Newtonian " through the ramparts of Paris and over the road paved with the huge cubes of granite and flint that formed the barricades behind which the insurgents fought in 1848, towards the

burial place of the kings of France. I will only say that I am surprised at his thinking of "game" in such a place. I should as soon thick of hearing a Scotch elder talk of seeliing a dram between morning and afternoon church service.—l am, sir, ke., ANGLO-SCOTIJS. Newington, London. P.S.—lt may interest those female readers of The Examiner who are to be distinguished or identified by that refrattory lock or curl of the hair that will not grow long enough to be bound up with the tresses, but will insist upon sporting itself on the forehead, that two of those sixteen widowers have got married, and that a third contemplates taking to himself a second wife. As the other thirteen will in all probability follow suit—(men in some things are just Ike sheep)—l give fair readers the hint. The "fines" will make a handsome pin-money prerent for the lady who secures the last man.

ANNUAL MEETING. Under the presidency of Lord Winmarieigh, the annual general meeting of the members of the Royal Manchester, Liverpool, and North Lancashire Agricultural Society to receive report of council and balance sheet; elect council and officers; to fix date of next year's show; agree upon the sum to be offered in prizes; select division of society in which the show of 1884 shall be held; revise rules and premiums, and conduct any other general business: was held at the Lion Hotel, Warrington, on Thursday. There was a good attendance, and amongst those present were Messrs. G. C. Hale, Knowsley; J. W. Fair, Wigan ; W. Derbyshire, Grappenhall ; J. Southern, Croft; W. Scotson, Aigburth ; J. White, Warrington ; R. Webster, Litherland ; P. Blundell and R. Catterall, Kirkham; J. Tunstall, Gar- stang ; T. FincLett, Tarporley, Thomas Rigby (sec.), *C. REPORT OF COUNCIL. The report of the Council for 1882, which was read by the Secretary, stated that the past year of the society's operations had been one of the most important of the many years of its existence. Nearly £3,000 had been awarded in prizes, divided into upwards of 200 classes, and embracing every varisey of live stock, farm produce, and implements. Special prizes were offered for " bast cultivated farms," and brought out 27 claimants, all of whom had their farms under superior management; the winning farms—especially those in the classes limited to arable cultivation, and those for daily farming and cattle grazing—being remarkable instances of high culture and efficient arrangement. The prizes for cattle were limited almost entirely7to,the society's district, bat they induced 2C3 claimants to join in competi- tion, the character of all being of great merit. The exhi- bition of horses, particularly that of stallions and brood mares in the classes of cart horses, was worthy of the best of our societies, and the show of sheep, pigs, poultry, and farm produce was even better than usual. The interest evinced in the exhibition of cheese and butter must have been encouraging to makers, and the Council hoped it might be a stimulant to them to try to make further im- provement in quality. It was to be regretted that a large proportion of English-made butter and cheese was only of second or third-class merit. The exhibition o'f agricultural implements was also very I large, and contained several extensive collections sent by I local agents, and several novelties of some value to agricul- ture. A large exhibition of machinery for the manufacture of cotton textile fabrics was made by the operative spinners of Preston, and added some interest to this part of the show; as also did two large museums of farm and garden seeds, grasses, bulbs, &c.; and some collections of fine shrubs, flowering plants, and seed potatoes, etc. The finan- cial success of the exhibition was considerable, but would have been greater had it not been for the increased cost of preparation consequent upon the wet weather that preceded the show, and the continuous rain which fell on the opening day. The balance in favour of the society was increased from £2,547, 2s. 31 to £2,819 us. 3d., which was £272 9s. more than last year, and represented the profit on the yeei's transaction. The Preston Local Committee fulfilled their promise to subscribe £l,OOO towards the prizes and expenses, and added £2C3 from their surplus subscriptions, making the total amouat of their contributions £1,207. The names of 49 gentlemen had been erased from the list of members in consequence of death or resignation, but 73 new names had been added to it, and the number of members now stood at 804. The Council, in grateful recognition of the honour long done to the society and the services rendered to the cause of agriculture generally by the Right Hon. Lord Win- marleigh, had elected his Lordship a life member and hon. vice-president. At the last meeting of the society, it was decided to hold next year's show at Liverpool, if the Mayor and Corporation of that city would receive the proposal favourably, and a committee was appointed to wait upon the Mayor to request this honour. The committee reported that they were kindly received by his Worship, and were promised his geocroffices in introducing the proposal to the Town Council, and in assisting to form a local committee. The noble CRA.IRMAN, who was greeted with applause, said they had the report, and he beggsd to move that it be re- ceived, adopted, and approved by their, with the exception of one paragraph in it relating to himself. However, it was a very flattering one for him, and he took that opportunity of saying how much obliged he was by its having been sug- gested. He had long been a member of that society. He felt that he was the oldest member in the room—in fact, the oldest member trf the society, with which he had been con- nected for half a century. (Applause.) Their last meeting, as the report said, had been the most favourable that he could recollect, since he had been a member. On the whole everybody who was present at Pr lston, bethought, must say that it was really as satisfactory as a public meeting could be, with the exception of the damage done to the ground and the difficulty of attending the meeting the first day owing to the weather. With that exception it really was successful throughout, as they all knew, and it was not only the opinion of the members of the society, but he happened to have the acquaintance of a great number of distinguished people who came from different parts of the country, and they every one of them expressed to him how gratified they were with what they saw at that meeting. In regard to the paragraph abeht the Duke of Albany, it was proposed that an address slaceold be presented to the Duke of Albany and the Duke of Cam- bridge, and he took the opportunity of presenting them. The Duke of Albany was still an invalid, but it gave the Duke of Cembridge great delight to come to the show. He had got a letter from the Puke of Cambridge, and it was gratifying to find that His. Royal Highness was so satisfied with the reception he met with. He told him privately before he went that his reception had been much beyond anything he bad expected in a part of the country where comparatively he was -so thtle known. There were several things 'connected with the society which on an occasion like the present he should refer to. The general state of agriculture and a great many things were growing deeply interesting to agri- culturists—landlords and tenants. He had no doubt in the fumre session of Parliament there were a great many agricul- tural subjects which must come under discussion in which they were all vitally interested. (Hear, bear.) He had no doubt there would be considerable difference of opinion on some points, but there were other points on which he would venture to say there would be no difference of opinion either as regarded landlord or tenant. So far as he could hear, in every part of the country there was an unanimous feeling that the tenants should have the advantage of any outlay ' they made on their farms, and it should be secured to them in the most substantial manner. (Hear, hear.) He did not think there would be any difference of opinion on that point. As to the. mode of doing it, and the mode in which tenancies should be conducted, of course there would bea variety of opinions, 'bat he had not the slightest doubt it wculd be discussed in the way agricultural questions were discussed in this I country—with good feeling between landlords and tenants. He himself should look with the greatest favour on every- thing that would conduce to the prosperity of the tenantry of this country, on whom he believed the prosperity of the country \reef greatly depended—much more than many people thought. Indeed - the agriculture of this country ' must be maintained in prosperity, or this coun's y woe' suffer, and it behoved both landlords and tenants to look at it in that way, and each consider in what way they could I promote it. There were one or two things which had been under the discussion at the council meeting, and perhaps lie ought to inform them their prizes seemed to have generally given great satisfaction. As the report said the farms that had gained prizes had been a credit to the society; but there had boon one, if not more, pretest against the prizes that were given. At their council meeting the other day, one gentleman who was second in the class for the best thorough-bred stallion, protested against the prize being given to Mr. Dodson on the ground that it was not a thorough-bred horse. They went into the question, and had great difficulty in deciding, and at last they came to the conclusion that on the whole it would be better to support the award of their judges. They had had notice from that gentleman that he intended to take legal proceedings against the society, and, of course, they_would have to stand the shot, and do the best they could in the matte. (Laugh- ter.) He had no doubt they had come the right decision-- but, of course, they were subject to a decision of a higher authority in the matter—and he had no. doubt they would be satisfied with any course the council might take on the subject. They would have in the course of the day the task of fixing the district for the meeting in 1984. They's had already fixed, as they kney, on Liverpool for 1883, and it would be for them to consider in what part of the district they would like the meeting of 1581-to be. He be- lieved there were several portions of the district that would be very glad to receive the society, but that they would discuss afterwards. Upon the whole he congratulated them yety much upon the stete of the society. Pt was in a most flourishing condition; it was founded on a enost satisfactory basis; and he thought there could not be a doubt in any man's mind that they were doing the good intevded when the society was founded. He could not believe that the prizes which the society had given had no effect, but he believed if the attentinn of the agriculturists in the county was drawn to the one object of their meetings such as that and the show meetings it would be doing a great good in the county. As regarded the improvement in stock, everybody must see what im- provements bad taken place. He did not suppose there was any part of England which could show better stock than they could in several parts of the county, arid they could recollect the time when Lancashire did not hold a high position in that respect. Their agriculture was improving. There was a great deal of drainage, and a great deal of attention was paid to the improvement of the land. He thought everybody driving through this county—the trylde district or any part—must see the great improvement that had taken place, and he did not think it was too much to flay that it was taking place in connection with that society. (Applause.) He moved the adoption of the report with the exception of the paragraph relating to himself. Mr. HALE, in seconding, said the Chairman had been most persistent in his efforts to promote the interests of the society, and he believed it owed more to him than to any other member for its present position. He thought this was a fitting occasion to make Lord Winmarleigh the fourth president, as they had none for the Northern district of the society. As to legislation he did not know what was coming, but as a rule they had better let things alone. No doubt there were reasons for legislation. His opinions were confined to a limited sphere, and in that sphere he had been connected with men who dealt fairly with their tenants, and in the estate he had the honour to look after, very little legislation was required. But he bad no doubt, from what he saw elsewhere, legisla- tion was required, and he only hoped whatever legislation there might be might be conducted with justice to all '

div.head: RE-ELECIION OF OFFICERS.
div.p: RE-ELECIION OF OFFICERS.

Messrs. Smeatham and R. Holland were re-elected respec- tively chemist and botanist to the society, and the offer of each gentleman to read a paper to the members was accepted. The CHAIRMAN, in moving the re-election of Mr. Rigby as secretary, stated that he was with him a good deal during the Guild week, and he was sure no one could have been more assiduous in the duties of his office than Mr. Rigby was. (Hear, hear.) The motion having been agreed to, Mr. FAIR asked whether there should not be something more than a vote of thanks given to .the secretary. Mr. Jouli WHITE moved that Mr. Rigby's salary be in- creased from £2OO to £230.

The CAAIRFAN quite agreed that Mr. Rigby's duties were very onerous and that they required great talent, great per- severance, and great industry, and all these were found in Mr. Rigby, whose services were very much to the interest of the society. The motion was unanimously carried.

div.head: FATAL RAILWAY ACCIDENT AT
div.p: THE FATAL RAILWAY ACCIDENT AT
WIDNES.

Mr. T. W. Barker, the deputy coroner, held an inquest at the Golden Ball Inn' Moss Bank, Widnes, on Tuesday morning, touching the death of Thomas Howell, who was killed on the Sheffield and Midland railway on Friday last, under circumstances reported in our last issue.—Mr. Robinson, of the locomotive department of the Manchester, Sheffield, and Liecolnshire Railway at Brunswick; Mr. Mitchell, traffic inspector, Midland Railway, Woodley ; and Mr. Patten, station master, Widnes, watched the proceedings on behalf of the Company. Ellen Howell said she was the widow of the deceased, who was 39 years of age, and lived at No. 4, Railway- street, Dukinfielci, near Manchester. He was a railway con- tractor's labourer, and worked on the Manchester, Sheffield, and Lincolnshire line. He left home on Friday morning about a quarter-past seven to go to Guide Bridge to ascer- tain whether he had to go to work at Widnes, where he had worked before. That was the.last time she saw him alive. She heard of his death at one o'clock on the afternoon of the day on which it occurred. He had worked on the rail- way four years. Joseph Smith, stonemason, in the employ of the Man- chester, Sheffield, and Lincolnshire Railway, said ke and the deceased were engaged in repairing a turntable near to the locomotive shed at the Tanhouse crossing. They both travelled together from Guide Bridge to Widnes on Friday morning. On arriving at Widnes, the inspector stopped the witness to inform him of some work he wished him to do; and whilst they were talking to4ether, the deceased walked .to his work along the railway. The servants of the company were allowed-to walk on the line, but there was a rule that a person doing so should always walk on the "off " or right , hand side, so that he would be in no danger from a train following behind him, and could see those coming in front. He believed the deceased was walking in the "Six foot." He should not have been there. He foand the deceased lying in the "four foot" on the up line. He had apparently only just been killed, and the brains protruded through the skull, which was fractured. It was his opinion that the deceased had been struck down while crossing from one side of the line to the other, in order to reach the place where he was working. He (witness) gave the alarm to the police, and the body was removed to the Golden Ball. He believed the deceased only was to blame for the acci- dent.—Mr..Mitchell said, in reply to a,juryman, that so far as they were aware, no person actually saw the occurrence. In reply to ofter que-tione, witness said it was not foggy at the time. He did not hear the driver of the train, which passed him about a quarter of a mile below where the acci- dent happened, whistle.—A Juryman : I don't think it is ' e driver's duty to whistle where the deceased was killed.— The Cornier: It is his duty to whistle when he sees anyone in front.—The Juryman: The driver did not see him, perhaps. John Henry Gorton, foreman porter on the Sheffield and Midland Railway, Widnes, said he had occasion to be at the goods station on 'Friday morning. He did not see the deceased before he was killed, but Tic hl,aved he was the first to examine the rails. Tie thou ht the train—the 9-30 Widnea to Warrington—which killed the deceased was travelling about sixteen miles an hour when it passed the point where he was standing. He noticed the engine whistle when passing the crossing, but he did not hear any alarm whistle.-.-.A Juryman: If the driver had been looking in front of his engine, as he ought to have been,. would he have seen the deceased ?—lt was rather foggy. It was impossible to see more than 30 or 40 yards.—The Juryman said it was absurd to say the train was only travelling 16 miles an hour, because it could not at that speed perform its journey in the time stated in the time table. He had seen them travelling very much quicker than that round the curve.—The Foreman : If it comes to that they are allowed to travel more.—The Juryman: Yes. Then what is the use of arguing about that P—Mr. Mitchell said it was scarcely fair to say the witness was not telling the truth. He thought he was telling the truth to the beet of his knowledge.—The Coroner observed that he did not think the juryman intended to impeach the veracity of the witness.

Jacob Holt, engine driver, in the employ of the Manches- ter, Sheffield, and Lincolnshire Railway Company, said he was driver of the 9.30 train from Widnes to Warrington, on Friday morning. His first stopping place was Sankey. He was running tender first, which was an ordinary practice, and was not against the rules of the company. There was no turn table at Widnes station, nor at Warrington. Before ho approached the place where the deceased was killed he should be travelling about 15 miles an hour. It was foggy; at the time, and he did not see anyone in front. He could not see quite so well going tender first as he could eagine first, but he could see sufficiently well to notice anything on the line. 11 He did not know that anything had happened until he got to Warririgton, where a telegram had been sent. When he was running from Widnes to Sankey he saw a great deal of dust flying, and when he arrived at the latter place be examined his engine. He found the framework covered with cemeni, and he thought then that something had happened. —ln answer to a juryman, witness said running engine first he atould perhaps see the rails at 14 yards distant from the engine, and tender first perhaps not for 30 yards. He did not think he could have seen the deceased that morning even if he had been travelling engine first. Mr. Robinson said it was. compulaory that the engines should run tender first under existing circumstances. In summing up the Coroner said upon this evidence he thought there could be no doubt that the unfortunate man was struck down by a passing train, and it was equally certain that it was the 9-30 train from Widnes. He thought they must also come to the conclusion that the occurrence was, accidental because, the deceased had a right to be there, being in the employ of the railway; but it seemed he had not been sufficiently cautious. If they thought that was so, they could not say that anyone but the tinfortunate deceased was to blame, for no one knew better than he that this train would come directly after him. With regard to the question of engines travelling tender first, he had no doubt that railway companies avoided it as much as possible, but still it was a matter of necessity in some cases, and it appeared to be so on this line, there not being sufficient turntables. If the jury thought more turn- tables ought to be provided and no engine run tender first,
chat was another quertion. No blame could be attached to the driver for running tender first, for it was the practice to do so.

A discussion took place with reference to running tender first, and a juryman suggested that the difficulty might be get over by running tank engines.—Mr. Robinson pointed out that that class of engine could not carry much water, but said it was under consideration whether to erect a water column at each end of the platform at Widnes station, and work the service with tank engines. A verdict of "Accidental death" was recorded.

div.head: MEDICAL AID ASSOCIATION.
div.p: MEDICAL AID ASSOCIATION.

TEA PARTY AND BALL. The Friendly societies' Medical Aid Association held a tea party and ball in the Public Hall, Warrington, on Mon- day evening, but the attendance was far below what was anticipated, owing, probably, to the very unfavourable state of the weather. The tea was an excellent one, and was served in a praiseworthy manner. A meeting held after- wards was presided over by His Worship the Mayor (Coun- cillor J. Crosfield), and he was supported by Messrs. John Hughes (president of the Association), Edward Whitehead (vice-president), William Bibby, S. Dunbobbin, A. Stirrup, Peter Langley, and W. Miller (members of the Association); and Alderman Burgess, Messrs. T. Bircball, Henry Roberts' and other gentlemen. Letters of apology had been received from Sir R. A. Cross, M.P., Mr. McMinnien, M.P., the ex- Mayor (Alderman Pickmere), Alderman Davies, Messrs. J. C. Parr, S. Reynolds, J. Marton, G. Crosfield, Rigby, Brook (town clerk), and others. The theAlleltale said some people thought the mayor of a borough like Warrington could do just what he liked. In His short experience he found that he could not do as he liked, but he had frequently to do as he was told. When Mr. Dunbobbin asked him to be present at that meeting he had to come because he felt it his duty as Mayor to sup- port an association like the present one. He was not aware until he received the invitation that Such an association existed in Warrington, but he was pleased that they had got such a large number of subscribers as 2,000. He had had five and thirty years' experience among working people, and he had always found that it was a difficult task to teach workingmen to be provident and lay something aside lor a rainy day, and it was very pleasing to him to find that there were 2,000 men so provident as to be sub- scribing to a medical aid association in case of sickness. The object of the association, he thought, must have the sympathy-of all right-thinking men. The very fact of a man subscribing to that institution was a proof that he was a respectable member of society, and he would dare to say that he would never find any member of the association brought up at the police .court for drunkenness. (Applause.) He expressed his sorrow that the weather had been so unfavourable, and said that it had undoubtedly prevented a great many from being present, and he concluded by saying that the association had his hearty support. (Applause.) • Mr. S. DUNBOBBIN spoke of the increasing popularity of such institutions as the Medical Aid Association, and said they were becoming more numerous throughout the country. Similar associations to the one named had been started at Birkenhead, Derby, Nottingham, and Lincoln, and their object was a worthy one. It was the means of making working men more provident, and caused them to band to- gether to help one another; and its influence would doubt- less have a-wholesome effect on the community at large, for the more interest working men took in these institutions the more Intelligent would they become. The subscription was very small, being one shilling per ,quarter, and for this sum they could have as good medical attention as could bepro- cured in the town. Mr. T. Bsncerete congratulated 'those present most ein- cerely on the admirable institution they had formed, which, hesai d, shasved that its members were of a provident and careful turn of mind, and would, therefore, be better citizens andjhe had no doubt that the association would be the means of lessening the poor-rate. He was very glad to be with them, and he only felt sorry that the state of the weather had caused their numbers to be smalL but he remarked that very many great and good things had to be supported and carried on by a few earnest men and women. In conclusion he wished the association every success. Alderman BURGESS congratulated them on the very judicious course of associating themselves together to pro- vide against sickness, and said that he had not known in his experience an institution that commended itself more thoroughly to hie judgment than the present one did. (Ap- plause.) In his opinion it was a step in advance of the crclinary insurance societies. He thanked them for asking him to be present, and stated that he would be glad to co- operate with them and assist them in any way that be could. (-Applause.) Mr. H. ROBERTS also addressed the meeting, and said that he believed the institution, in whose behalf they were met, was one which deserved ,and ought to command the support of every ratepayer in the town. Mr. HUGHES- proposed, and Mr. WHITEHEAD seconded, a vote of thanks to the Mayor, which was heartily accorded. The rest of the evening was devoted to dancing, Mr. Knights band being in attendance.

A " PCiPI3I." DUFFICULUES.—Thos. Pope was, at the Prescot Petty Sessions, on Tuesday, summoned to si.ow cause why he did not pay £4 19s. arrears, dee from him to the Board of Guardians for the maitatenance of his mother. —Mr. Hartley, clerkto the Prescot Union, stated that he was instructed by the Gnardians to ask for an order upon the defendant to pay £4 19s. arrears due under an order made by that court on the 16th August for the payment by defen- dant of 3s. a week towards the maintenance of his mother. He paid up to May last, but since that time he had ceased paying, and owed £4 19s. He was a mastfr blacksmith at Earlestown, employing five men and boys, including his two sons. His mother was 75 years of age, and was not ex- pected to live long. She was receiving ss. a week from the Union, 21. if which was repaid by defendant's brother, who also provided the old woman with a home at Tarbock.— Thomas Parkinson, relieving officer, having given evidence, defendant said he had been in great difficulties for some time. In two years he had been involved in thirteen bank- ruptcies, his claims under which amounted to £9,000, and he had lost upwards of £3OO under them besides having had other losses. He also stated that he had had to pay £l9 for the amputation of the hand of one of his sons, who had met with an accident, and he had also to pay £32 medical expenses incurred by another son getting his thigh hurt.— The Bench made the order asked for, allowing the defendant till the end of January to pay the money.

div.head: GOOD SAMARITAN..
div.p: THE GOOD SAMARITAN..
LECTURE AT RUNCORN BY THE REV. PETER bIACKENZIE.

In behalf of the circuit fund, the Rev. Peter MacKenzie, the popular lecturer, preached a sermon to a crowded congre- gation in St. Paul's Wesleyan chapel, on Monday afternoon. In the evening the rev, gentleman lectvred on "The Good Samaritan; a true type of Christian philanthropy." The hall was well filled. Mr. Robert Garnett, of Warrington, occupied the chair, and he was supported on the platform by the Revs. Go. Hack, S. Meer, J. Billirc,rton, J. Picknell, Williams; Messrs. Jno. Simpson, Geo. S. Hazlehurst, T. Norman, T. Simister, R. Norm9n, H. Randle, an S. C. Beckett.

The CEP TRY N raid he had received a leUer from the Rev. W. Preston, thanking the committee for kindly send- ing him a ticket for the platfoLm for that evening's lecture, but a previous engrgemen which he had made fora lee'zure in Lis own school-room, prevented his attentlanca ; and he, therefore, sent an apology. In in;..oducirc, the lecturer, the Chairman thanked them for the honour they he done him in asking him to take the chair that r'ght. (A r,lause.) He was not quite Or— whether the lectures which so distinguished the present day, d not to some extent tend to stultlfy and cripple the time and patience which we should give to the study, of the subject ourselves. He sometimes had the impression that lectures made people lazy, when they could go to a meetirg like the present and listen to the condensed thoughts "of a lecturer like Mr. MacKenzie, whom he now introduced.

The LECTURER, who was received with loud applause, commenced by giving an eloquent and humorous review of the various lectures he had delivered, and referring to Jonah, said he liked to deliver that lecture about conference time. Jonah, when the Lord appointed him to a new circuit, wgnted to start a shopkeeping as a little business of his own—(laughter)—and after paying his fare and tumbl- ing iato his bunk, had the bum bailiffs sent after him by the Lord. (Laughter.) Jonah did not like his new appoint- ment, and went and joined the member for Nornhamptonz (Loud laughter and applause') All due respect to the mem- ber for Northampton; but he did. Jonah went down as far as Joppa, and took a pasnge on board a ship for another place, 10-t when the "bums" threw him overboard the big fish sidled up towards him, and seemed to say "Con in out of the wet, brother." (Much laughtcr.) He assurel them that the fish had the worst of it. It was poorly all the time it had him. (Renewed laughter.) There was such groaning and growling and grumblirg.—Jonah was holding a public service all by himself. (Laughter.) He did both the singing and praying together and read the lessons.; and the fish was glad to get rid of him. When he did get rid of him Jonah did not want a second appointment to that place. (Much laughter.) He sometimes thought that if the stationing committee would procure a big tank and a big fish, when the brethren were debating where they were to go, it would expedite the appointments considerably. (Applause.) He had spoken of Esther, the diamond with- out a flaw; of Ruth, the moss rose of Moab; but now that he was getting older himself he had parted with these old friends, and he had come down to the New Testament, where he had mat with the Good Samaritan, a noble type of Christian philanthropy. He should first look at his home, Samaria; secondly at his children—he was a good Samaritan; and thirdly at his characteristics. The rev, lecturer then gave a sketch of the geogEaphical position of Palestine, and a historical sketch of Samaria, alluding to the hatred which existed between the Jews and the Samaritans. Elihu Burritt had said that if all the hatred and animosity and spleen that was ever felt and expressed by enemy, r %lions, caste, and colour, were condensed into one element of ani- mosity, it would be milk and water compared with tbe hatred the Jew had in his breast towards the poor Samari- tan. He would neither drink of his well, taste of the food of his table, nor giye the ordinary salutation of good morn- ing. He blocked up every avenue of restoration. He denied him the privilege of repentance. The Samaritan was the only being out of pandemonium who could not have access to the Jewish religion by becoming a proselyte. And they would leave him there. They buried his dcathless soul be- low the hearing of the resurrection trumpet, they anathema- tised his body, and excommunicated him from the resurrec-

don of the dead. The doctor who went to Christ with the questien, "Good Master, what shall I do to inherit eternal life ?" was a good sort of fellow, but it was no use to tell him that the Samaritan was his neighbour; so he told him of the man that went down from Jerusalem to Jericho. The

lecturer gave a graphic description of the journey from Jeru- salem to Jericho, a distance of 18 miles, remarking that when a traveller wished to traverse it he had to get a dozen of the biggest scoundrels and cut-throats he could find to escort him. The other scoundrels then knew that they must get out of the way, for there were bigger scoundrels than they to meet them. (Laughter.) Weil. a Jew started alone, and when he had travelled perhaps 13 miles some robbers pounced upon him, and stripped him, of more of his clothes than they did his skin. The robbers, remembering that dead men tell no tiles, killed the Jew, as they thought, end left him for dead. The poor fellow lay there, he could Lot tell how long, when he heard footsteps. Presently his own spiritual advisers came round the corner. 0, that was grand. It was his own priest. 0, what kind providence had sent this blessed man, who had that morning offered up a sacrifice and eaten the young pigeons to his breakfast. (Liughter.) But the priest was a man who could keep his head on—a cool man in a crisis. He took a glimpse at the wounded man, whose heart's blood -vitas flowing, and thought "he is too far gone, it is impcssible to cure him, and it would be cruelty to shift him. He must die in peace. It would be a risky, thing to try to save, and he must not risk his invaluable life for a man three parts dead already." And besides, there was a second preacher —his young colleague, the Levite, coming after him—and r mild look after him. And as he had to open a mission at Jeticho, it would be unseemly to go before a respectable audience besmeared with blood 'and dust. He must leave him to a Lind Providence and to his undergraduate who was coining after him. (Laughter.) And he left that man with the blood gurgling from his gory wounds. Human blood! worth more than "all the blood of beasts'en Jewish altars slain." Then came the Levite, who lived near the Jew in a detached villa, and took the service when his _

superior officer was not present. (Laughter.) The Levite looked upon him with sympathy, but it was very inoperative. He sympathiscl with him' but sympathy without relief was just like mustard without beef. (Loud laughter.) Had he been there he would have called upon ti.te man to stop, and put an armful of moss under his head, to give him a drink of water from the flowing spting, to put a palm leaf over his gaping wounds to stop the sun from broiling his blood. But no, be could not stop; his superior officer had not thought fit to stop, and so. he must not, for he had to hasten on to hear that superior officer preach from the Book of Job on the text : "I delivered the poor that cried and the fatherluc' t and him that had none to help him," and, besides, he had promised him faithfully that if the or- ganist was not present, he would start the tunes. (Loud laughter.) He would have shouted to him : Stop, if you have a human heart, and not an icicle. Stop, if you have a soul not as destitute of feeling as the figure-head of a ship. The wounded Jew would despair; but, by-the-bye came the Samaritan, of whom the Jew was in great dread lest he should kill him. The mule gave a great snort, and the Samaritln said " Whoa, Anthony. Whoa, Anthony,"-- (much laughter)—and as soon as the Samaritan saw a man bleeding_ . death, he said. " Great father _ .

Joseph, what's 4; ?" (Loud laughter.) At once national prejudices were laid aside, and jumped off his mule, rushed towards the Jew, and poured in his wounds oil and wine. He then put him upon his ass and carried him to Jericho, where he nursed him in an inn and paid for his lodging until he was recovered from his wounds. Christ then hurried to the lawyer and inquired " which of these, thinkest thou, was the neighbour unto him that fell among thieves ?" The lawyer would not say the Samaritan. He would not put the word into his mouth. No, he would rather put a toad into it. (Laughter and applause.) Bnt he could say he that showed mercy upon him. Then it was not the priest nor the Levite. It was the Samatitan ; and Jeps said, "Go thou and do like- wise." We needed to catclf something of the spirit of the Good Samaritan. Some people never could find a cause or person worthy of their charity. The politician, the philo- sopher, and the poet had each their vocation, and so had the noble philanthropist, who would ever find something worthy of his assistance. (Applause.) It was the spirit of the philanthropist that needed to be cultivated. The Good Samaritan was entirely above national prejudice and religious bigotry, he had not such a thing in his entire .calibre. When the lifeboat men in Yarmouth were called out, they did not inquire who were to be saved, but set to work to save them. When the firemen were called out in Bradford, did they ask if it it was an Irish, Scotch, or English family that had to be saved? No. They put the fire out and saved the people, and then made the inquiry. (Applause.) If a poor half-e-rved and half-clad fellow-creature went to their doors and asked for aid, they could not think of saying "Do you attend St. Paul's." (Laughter and applause.) Give her half a* pint of cocoa, and then she would tell where she attended. And if she did not attend any- where, she wanted • warming. (Applause.) While our common humanity commanded us to look after the bDdy, the religion of Jesus Christ commanded them to look after the soul. Religion was a large-hearted thing. The man who, looking through his telescope at the heavens, thought he saw the Lord making new worlds, which were coming helter skelter down. He determined to clean his glasses, and have a bettgr view, before he published this new phenomena to the werld, when, 10, he found two flies had impeached the integrity of the universe. (Laughter.) Some of the churches wanted their mental discs wiping, so that they might see clearly. Their religion was a Catholic, a living and a practical religion, and not an ethereal dream. The Good Samaritan lost much of his valuable time, and made tome sacrifice while parting with his oil and wine, but he found the luznry of doing good amply repaid him. Heaven and earth would conspire to bless that man's example, and he trusted they would all be at last lifted up and placed by kis side. The lecturer resumed his seat amid long-continued applause. Mr. &MISTER niovcd, and Mr. G. S. HAZLELIIIRST seconded,
that the sincere and hearty thanks of the audience be ten* dered to MA MacKenzie for his lecture.

The motion was carried with acclamation. Mr. "MacKENzrE replied, remarking that since May last 151 had travelled 8,000 miles, delivered 85 lectures, preached 1 , sermons, and collected £3,000, and he was still well an° hearty, and prepared to do God's work. (Applause.) A similar compliment having been paid to the Chaim:olh on the motion of Mr. MACKENZIE, seconded by Mr. T. NO MAN, concluded the meeting.

Larkin desired to be taken to Crewe less in those days, and there were not so many people Hospital, but Dr. MacDougall decided that he should to travel. Travelling by coach was very expensive, be conveyed to the Liverpool Infirmary; where he and only a few people could be conveyed by all accompanied him. He died shortly after his arrival. the coaches even on the most important roads in the The deceased leaves a widow and one child. country. A gentleman recently had told him that 83 coaches passed through Warrington every day, besides great numbers of post chaises and private carriages. If they went back into the last century there was a still greater contrast to the present. Sedan chairs were then very com- mon in many towns. For the use of these regular fares were fixed just as they were now arranged for cabs. Till so recently as three hundred years ago travelling was done almost entirely on horseback. In the reign of Queen Anne there were no public conveyances of .any kind, and there were only one or two main lines of road in the country. In 1619 a tax equal to £2OO of our money was levied on all persons below a certain rank who kept a coach. Except on the main roads almost all the traffic of the country was carried by pack-horses, that used to go in gangs of 40 or 50, following each other in a line, con- ducted by a leader with a bell bung round his neck. At the beginning of the 17th century the communica- tion between one place and another was so tedious that a letter from Yorkshire to Oxford could scarcely be answered in less than a month. In 1754 a company of merchants at Manchester started a new vehicle, called the "flying coach," as it was to be run at five miles an hour, and the advertisement said "However incredible it may appear, this coach will actually (barring accidents) arrive in Lon- don in four days and a half after leaving Manchester." (Laughter.) By rail the journey was accomplished in from four to five hours. In 1757 another " flying machine on steel springs" was set up by the merchants of Liverpool, which beat the Manchester coach, perform- ing the journey in three days. Sheffield and Leeds, and other places soon after set up coaches, and by 1784' they actually managed to travel eight miles an hour. Forty years since a passenger boat left Runcorn every morn- ing for Manchester, where it arrived in seven hours. ' it was a great convenience to petsons living anywhere near to the canal, as they conld get on board or a light at any point they wished. A similar boat left Manchester for Runcorn. An omnibus left Chester every morning for Preston ~Brook, arriving there in time for the boat going to Manchester, and it left again for Chester on the arrival of the boat from Maachester in the afternoon. , This omnibus continued to run till the railway to Chester was opened in 1851. For some years what were called swift boats ran instead of the old slow ones, between Run- corn and Manchester, leaving each place in the morning and getting back at night. At that time, and for many years previously, one or more passenger steamers left Liver- pool each day, coming up to Runcorn with the tide and re- maining for a short time, and then going back with tho tide to Liverpool. Before the Old Quay Canal was bought by the Bridgewater Trustees two passenger steamers used to run, the "Duke of Bridgewater" and the "Eclipse," and there was a great amount of rivalry and competition displayed. From the opening of the Liverpool and Manchester railway 52 years since. the nearest station to the Runcorn Ferry was Rainbill. Describing the journey from Chester to Runcorn, via. Liverpool, the lecturer said passengers sometimes went by a carriage which was attached to a train of coal waggons going from Runcorn Gap to St. Helens, and when they got near to Sutton, where they crossed the,Liverpool and Man- chester line, the train stopped, and they scrambled down the embankment and took their chance of the first train for Liverpool or Manchester, as the ease might be. When the railway was made from Widnes to Garston, and to Warring- ton, things soon became very different. The extension from Speke to Liverpool was a great boon; but, of course, the greatest change of all was made by the building of the Runcorn railway bridge, placing Runcorn on the main line between Liverpool and London. In these days there was no bank in Runcorn, and for years he used to take a parcel two or three mornings a week to the trusty old captain, Peter Yates, for him to take to the bank at Warrington, and to meet the boat in the afternoon for the parcel he would bring back. At length there was a bank opened once a week, and ultimately every day, as it is now. Having referred to mail coaches, the lecturer related some humorous details respecting dress, in the course of which he stated that he remembered at one time when he was a boy, his clothes were so tight it was almost like skinning an eel taking them off, and his trousers were so tightly strapped down it was hard work to stoop to pick any- thing from the floor, and to sit straight on a chair for half an hour made his knees ache dreadfully. The contrast between what we were accustomed to, and the state of things 50 or 60 years ago, in many of the commonest arrangements of life was very great. The introduction of matches was mentioned, and he gave a humorous sketch of the difficulties under which our forefathers laboured in obtaining a light with a flint and steel and a tinder box. Several tinder boxes of various styles were shown. He touched upon the invention of gas, steel pens, and blotting paper, narrating in an attractive way how things were previously. When he was a boy the postage on letters was a very serious item if many of them were received. A letter 1 oz. in weight, which was now id., would, 60 years, since, be 4s. to London. There were no envelopes in those dais.. Letters were generally written on sheets of what were quarto post, that was the large letter sheets. One side had to be left blank as it had to be folded up and the address written on the outside with a wafer or sealing wax. Members of Parlia- ment could frank letters for their friends; that was, by writing their name outside, the letter went free. Friends who were going a journey often had lots of letters to take charge of, and there was generally written in the corner" Favour by Mr. So and So." Now, as they all knew, a letter of loz. went for a penny without regard to distance. Mr. Simpson concluded by referring to the tax on newspapers, giving some interesting quotations from Mr. Chambers reminiscences. The more he (the lecturer) knew about the past the more thankful he was that his lot had been cast in these days, rather than a few years earlier, and the energy and enterprize of the present led one to think that before many years had passed aivay farther chaeges, perhaps as great as any in the past, would be seen. Mr. Simpson took his seat amid loud applause, which had been frequently awarded to him during the reading of his lecture. A vote of thanks was accorded to Mr. Simpson for his ex- cellent lecture, on the motion of Mr. CRAIK, seconded by the Rev. W. PRESTON, and a similar compliment was paid to the Chairman on the motion of Mr. LAKE.
ACTION AGAINST THE RUNCORN SOAP AND ALKALI COMPANY.

At the Birkenhead County Court yesterday (Friday), Mr. Wynne Ffoulkes, judge, gave judgment in an action brought by John Cronshaw, as next-of-kin of Wm. Cronshaw (a minor), against the Runcorn Soap and Alkali Company to recover £l2O compensation for personal injury sustained by the plaintiff whilst in the employ of the defendants.—Mr. Little, barrister, appeared for the plaintiff, and Mr. Pickford for the defence. The hearing of the case was fully reported in our columns two or three weeks ago.— His Honour, in giving judgment, said that the plaintiff's ; case rested on the allegation that there was a defect in the I saw, and that the machinery was not in proper working 1 order, but ho did not consider that the evidence would sup-1 port that allegation. If had been proved that the saw was dull, but that was not a structural defect within the mean- ing of the Actiand would not confer on the plaintiff a right of action. Was the accident caused by the saw being dull, and on that point the only evidence was that given by the plaintiff himself, who thought that the saw came upon a , knot in the wood, and being dull, was unable to cut it, and! caused the wood to dance or jump up. Three witnesses' named Jones, Gerrard, and Williams stated that circular 1 saws like this in use required to be sharpened from three to 1 five times in a working day of nine hours, according to the 1 nature of the wood which it was at work upon. Another , man named Lowry thought three times a day sufficient,l and two others named Brown and Mitten said , that three or four times would be sufficient when cutting spruce, as the plaintiff was on the day in question. It appeared, however, that the ' saw had been sharpened nine days prior to the accident,' but had only worked three days in the interval, and not the whole of that time. It would therefore depend upon the work it had done to decide whether it would require sharpen- ing or not on the day in question. On the part of the de- fendant no practical sawyers were called, but Mr. Webster, who had had 16 years experience of saws, was called. He said that if it had only been worked three days in that time, the saw was perfectly safe to cut spruce with on the fourth day. Three men in the defendant's employ named Ward, Kilcross, and Kirkham, were called, and from their evidence it was stated that the saw was tested by Ward before it began work that morning, and Kilcross said that he worked it after the accident, and found it cut all right. The saw would lose all its cutting power by degrees for some time before it became unsafe and dangerous, but the evidence failed to satisfy.his (his Honour's) mind that it had arrived at that state at the time of the accident. Ward said be had tested it before the plaintiff began work with it, and that to the best of h s judgment it was sharp enough, and in proper order to do its work that day. If he came to that opinion really and honestly in the test which he made, even if his judgment proved erroneous, he did his duty, and could not be accused of negligence in ordering plaintiff to go and work at it. In conclusion His Honour said that the plaintiff had faVed to satisfy him that the injury was caused through any negligence on the part of the defendants or their workmen, and, though he deeply sympathised with him under the circumstances he must give judgment against him. His Honour then gave a verdict for the defendants with costa against the plaintiff's next friend.

div.p: HAP,TLAND 'WESLEYAN CHAPEL, WIDNES.
SALE OF

Now that Hartland Wesleyan Chapel is fast approaching completion, the members who 1/4vill worship within its walls are naturally turning their attention towards furnishing the interior with various appointments for their comfort and convenience. With the object of raising funds to accom- plish this end, a sale of work was opened in Oakland-street sclaool-room, on Thursday afternoon, by Mr. Benjamin Walker, of Earlestown. The building had undergone a com- plete and pleasing metamorphosis. At the entrance had been erected a porch, decorated with evergreens, while the interior was bright with adornments of many decorations, reflecting the highest credit upon Mr. W. Whitley, under whose directions the work had been carried out. Deftly executed mottoes, expressing a variety of sentiments, of which "Prosper Widnes Circuit" and "God save the Queen" were most prominent; bannerettes of many hues cleverly quartered shields of a variety of devices, covered; the walls of the room, and at one end the handsome proces- sional banner of the school formed a splendid back- ground. Amongst the numerous company at the opening ceremony there were present the Revs. R. Harper (superintendent minister), J. Tessytnan, Richards, Messrs. W. Hartland, B. Brawn, &c.—The Rev. R. HARPER delivered a short introductory speech, in which he adverted to the unpropitious state of the weather, and expressed his admiration of the effectiveness of the decora- tions, and concluding by calling upon Mr. Walker to open the bazaar. The latter gentleman then delivered a suitable address, and concluded by declaring the bazaar open. The stalls, which were arranged round the room, one occupying the centre, were laden with a great variety of articles of many textures and many colours, and upon which it was evident the deft fingers of the ladies of the congregation had been for a considerable time engaged in preparing. It is expected that from £7O to £BO will be realised. The ladies presiding on the "work stall" were Mesdames Hartland, Duxburv, Newall Bennett, and Rigby, Misses Rodgers and Wendt; the refreshment stall, Mesdames Proctor, W. Whitby, Knowles; Messrs. Jackson, Ankers, and Coomber. Fancy stall (1) : Misses Whitby, Frodsham, Nevrans, Brookes, Jones, and Briggs; (2) Mesdames Har- per, Rushton, Ankers, and Miss Harper. Misses A. Ankers, Davis, Pattinson, and Woodward were engaged in vending flowers. Messrs. Bailey, Hicks, and F. Whitby were busily engaged in carving at the refreshment stall, while Mrs. Brookes, T. Whitby, Ogden, Dodd, Gill, and Wainwright were fully occupied-in the mysteries of "cutting up." A special feature in the proceedings was the numerous enter- tainments which were provided. Messrs. Rodgers and Jack- son were lb charge of a microscope, with which they opened to the view of the spectators the motion of the new comet, while the wonders of the natural world were exhibited in a menagerie by Messrs. F. Harper and J. Chadwick; and Messrs. Ottier and Routledge were prepared to tell the weight of any person desirous of knowing. Believers in the powers of electricity could gratify their peculiar feelings by the aid of a galvanic battery, worked by Messrs. J. Jackson and H. Jackson. Mr. Duxbury proved an efficient judge of elocu- tion in the speaking bees which were held. During the afternoon andi evening the visitors were entertained by exhibitions of musical talent on the piano by Messrs. Ravenscroft, F. W. Whitby, A. D. Whitby, R. Briggs, Misses E. Ankers, A. Ankers, and Lord, Mr. Beswick, as exhibitor, and Mr. Watson, as lecturer, gave a magic lantern enter- tainment of a very superior description. As musical director, Mr. W. Whitby had arranged for a series of concerts, at which the choir, under his leadership, rendered in excellent style several choruses, the solos being taken by a number Df local vocalists of considerable ability,

div.p: W OR K.
FANCY BAZAAR AT FRODSHAM.

A fancy bazaar, in aid of the circuit funds, was held in the large school-room attached to Trinity Wesleyan Chapel, Frodsham. on Thursday and Friday. The opening cere- mony took place on Thursday afternoon, when we noticed the following amongst those present :—Revs. J. M. Bamford, J. R. Trotter, and D. Schofield; John Simpson, Esq. ; Messrs. Thomas Hadfield, Thomas Norman, W. H. Picker- ing, Samuel Walker, Robert Andrews, W. Collinson, Joseph Knibb, R. H. Turner, Thomas Sant, J. Yapp, John Lowe, R. Proud, J. S. Rimmer ; Mesdames Charles Reynolds, Bolderstone, Dunsford, Tapp, A. Thomas, Weaver, Edmonds, Andrews; Misses Simpson, Wrights, Rigbys, Borwick, Pretty, and Lewis.—The Rev. J. M. BAMFORD, in• commencing the proceedings, expressed his personal pleasure and satisfaction that the labours of the past six months had such a successful and happy consummation. The sale of work had not been instituted because of any special pressure in the circuit funds, as he was glad to say that there was no debt upon the chapels at Kingsley, Five Crosses, and Helsby, and there was a reserve fund in the bank ; but the income from the circuit did not allow for extraordinary expenditure, and it occurred to him that it would be a wise thing to take some steps for replenishing the reserve fund in the short term which remained of his ministration amongst them rather than leave it to a stranger. He had been much pleased to see the hearty and harmonious way in which the ladies and gentlemen had devoted themselves to this labour of love, and Mrs. Hadfield, Mrs. Collinson, Mrs. Robinson, and assistants deserved all praise for the excellent display before them. The work of the gentlemen of the committee spoke for itself, but Mr. Robinson and Mr. Fitton deserved their thanks for the artistic labour and skill shown in the decorations, and they had been ably assisted by Messrs. Gould and eon, Jones, Rowe, Samuel Sharp, and H. Smith. He had bad to do with bazaars where the results bad reached £2,000, but he had not seen decorations so tastefully and artistically carried out as on the present occasion. His pleasnre was greatly increased lsy the presence of Mr. Simpson, who had kindly and cheer- fully consented to open the proceedings of the day. Mr. SIMPSON said that when he was asked to open the bazaar he felt pleasure in complying, not because he liked 'to take such a prominent position but because be felt glad to have an opportunity of shelving a little more sympathy with Frodsham Wesleyans than ha was often able to do. Having referred to the object for which the bazaar had been undertaken, be said that in Wesleyanism there was no room for economising as they would do in a private family, they had to provide their minister's stipend and other matters, and if they attempted to economise they would probably be charged with stinting. (Hear, hear.) Methodism was a system of extension, they could not stand still, if they did so they generally found they were going back, and greater efforts would have to be made if a circuit must keep pace with the constant increase of members. The speaker advocated a system of general giving, and illustrated what could be done by a small additional weekly amount when spread over a large number of people. He wished every success to the bazaar, which was for a very good object, and he hoped the result would be everything that could be wished for. He had much pleasure in Ideclaring the bazaar open. (Applause.)—The decorations were of an unique character and represented six shops in the quaint half-timbered style, peculiar to early English architecture. The lattice windows were very realistic, and added considerably to the scenic effect. The arrangements conveyed the idea of a market-square on a festive occasion, and the gaily dressed ladies who flitted about gave it an animated appearance. The first shop was presidel over by Mrs. R. Andrews, Miss Junes, Misses Susie, Emma and Clara Hadfield, Miss Ethel Kent, and Messrs. R. Andrews and H. Smith. This shop contained an extensive assortment of plants, ferns, and flowers, which had been liberally contributed by Mrs. Pickering, Messrs. E. A. W [IVA, A. ruomas, Ttiomai raaanem, and It. Andrews. At the next three shops a variety of plain and fancy needlework, Japanese goods, [sc., drc., were tastefully displayed, and the following ladies presided :—Mesdames Hadfield, Moss, Fairhurst, Turner, Collinson, Robinson, and Proud. An old fashioned ivy-covered cottage was the reposi- tory for teNrs and other articles usually found at bazaars, and was presided over by Miss Walker, of Frodshani, and Miss Garnett, of Helsby. A plentiful supply of refresh- ments was provided at an ancient shop on which the year 1632 was recorded, and the following ladies were in charge of this branch of the fancy fair, viz.:—Misses Andrews, Edmonds, Proud, Turners, Challoner, Rimmers, Chew, Sharp, Nickson, Kenyon, Kent, Worth, Robinson, and Booth.

A varied musical programme was given during each day, and consisted of organ recitals by Messrs. J. Yapp and John S. Rimmer, and pianoforte solos and songs by members of the congregation and friends, and proved a pleasant source of enjoyment.

div.p: DISTRICT NEWS MIDDLE WICH.

TYE CHESHIRTE POACHING A/FRAY.—On Monday morn- ing four Northwich men, named Johnson, Aldersley, Sand- bach, and Hawke, were brought up at Middlewich, charged with night poaching and shooting with intent to murder Robert Niddrie, gamekeeper, and Sergeant. John Gosling, of the county constabulary. The police stated that Niddrie's gunshot wounds in the leg were still very serious, and that Hodgkinson, whose skull was fractured, was still unable to attend, and the investigation was again adjdurned.

div.head: THELWALL.
div.p: THELWALL.

For the purpose of disposing of the balance of the sub- scriptions raised to defray the expenses of holding meetings, kc., to discuss the best means of preventing the flooding of land adjoining the river Mersey, a meeting of the subscri- bers was advertised to be held in the Schoolroom, Thelwall, on Monday evening. The attendance, however, owing to the inclemency of the weather, was very small, and it was decided to postpone the meeting until Monday, the 18th Inst., at seven o'clock, when it is hoped there will be a good attendance. There are two or three suggesticns as to the disposal of We, balance, but the one which seems to meet with the greatest favour is that the £4 Bs. 4d. in hand shall go towards forming the nucleus of a farmers' subscription to the preliminary expenses of the Manchester Ship Canal project.

div.head: LYMM.
div.p: LYMM.

CHURCIT OF ENGLAND TEMPERANCE SOCIETY ENTER- TAINMENT.—On Tuesday evening, the monthly entertain- ment in connection with the above society was given by the members. A very lengthy and varied programme had been prepared, and, as the night was very fine, the room was crowded in every corner by an appreciative and attentive audience. The band, a usual, gave some fine selections. First on the list was a song by Mr. J. Bleese which was given in a very creditable manner. This was Poflowed by a recitation, after which the rector tang "Once again." During the evening the Misses Robinson gave in excellent style the pianoforte duet "Sleigh bells." This undoubtedly was the event of the night, the bells attached to the player's wrists being very effective, so effective, indeed, as to completely bring down the house. Next came a comic song, " Father of a family," by Mr. Oddie, who, on being recalled, gave "Wake up Johnny." Mr. Smith was very successful in his two songs the first one, "God bless our Sailor Prince," being much applauded. A pianoforte duet by the Misses Bayley, of Statham, was now given; after which Mr. Hall got upon the boards. His rendering of the reading "Lord Tom Noddy" was very good, as was also "The country- man's visit to London." Two readings by the Brothers Clare having been given, the entertainment was brought to a close by singing the Nationul Anthem. It may not be out of place to mention that the society is in a most flourishing condition, and that new members are added every meeting. On Tuesday night an " adul/ branch" was formed, with Mr. Hall as secretary, and we sincerely hope this branch will succeed as well as the juvenile. LYMM LOCAL BOARD.—The meeting of this Board was held on Thursday, when the members present were Messrs. Cameron (in the chair), Rogers, Forster, Gibson, Appleton, Callender, Ridgway (clerk), and Fox (medical officer.)—Dr. Fox said the sanitany inspector had prepared an account of his survey, which showed that 416 different inspections of properties had been made, and an account given of no less 1,016 houses. The sanitary arrangements of this large num- ber of houses were various, and some would meet with the approval of the Board, and others the Board would condemn. He suggested that the consideration of the matter be referred to a committee.—The suggestion, after a little consideration, was adopted.—Dr. Fox said that as far as he knew, the village was free from infectious disease. The Surveyor, in his repart, called attention to the dan- gerous condition of the bridge slope near the Whitborough aqueduct. It was now four months since the fence was broken down, and notwithstanding that the attention of the Navigation Company's engineer had been called to the matter, nothing had been done.—lt was decided that the clerk write Mr. Collier, of the Navigation Company, calling his attention to the dangerous condition of bridge slope, and asking that steps might be taken without delay to remedy the present unsafe condition.—This was all the , business of intewest.
LYMAt WESLEYAN BAND OF HOPE.-Mr. Pearson, of Man- cheater, delivered an address in connection with this society on Monday evening. The meeting was presided over by Mr. C. Brown.

ANOTHER GREAT FIRE IN LONDON. DESTRUCTION OF WAREHOUSES. OVER £2,000,000 DAMAGE. One of the greatest fires which has occurred in London for many years broke out yesterday morning. Wood-street, the scene of the disaster, is in the heart of the city, and almost every building is occupied by well-known firms. About half-past two a policeman noticed a light in the base- ment of Messrs. Foster, Porter, and Co.'s premises, and al- though an alarm was immediately given, the fire soon shot up through the building, and quickly spread to the ware- house of Messrs. Rylands and S.ns, the well-known Manchester firm. The whole block of buildings from Wood-street to Addle-street and Philip Lane then appeared to be one mass of flames, the dry Manchester goods giving such a hold to the fire that it was soon apparent that the adjoining buildings only could be saved, and that the whole block was doomed. The utmost efforts were made to prevent the houses on the op- posite side of the street from catching fire, and as large pieces of burning materials, light burning cotton fabrics and pieces of wood were flying in all directions, this was a! work of no small difficulty. However, by the most stren- uous efforts, the spread of the fire beyond the square block in which it first broke out was prevented. The flames in the meantime had passed beyond Messrs. Rylands and Foster Porter's premises, and seized hold on those of Messrs. Sargood and Co., and Fleming and Norton's jewellery establishment. These were soon one mss of seething flame; the contents of the buildings being as inflammable as those first attacked. The fire continued to rage till after nine o'clock, but it fortunately was confined to the block in which it originated. The wall of the consumed buildings in Wood- street fell outwards with a terrific crash, damaging the ware- houses opposite, but doing no further injury, the event having been foreseen by Captain Shaw, and the street having been cleared. At 10 o'clock the engines were still playing on the fire, which continued to burn in some places. Im- mense crowds assembled in the vicinity soon after the out- break, and remained until long after dawn. No accidents are reported involving serious injury or loss of life. There were a few persons sleeping on the premises, the most of them in the capacity of caretakers, but all ware rescued safely. The damage is estimated at between two and three millions sterling.

ST. lIELENS LITERARY AND SCIENTIFIC ASSOCIATION. On Taesday evening the first of a series of lectures to be given in connection with this association, was given in the Bro ok-street Independent schools, by Mr. Sherrock, St. Helens, on the spectroscope and its sees in foretelling the weather. Mr. J. C. Gamble presided, and there was an average attendance. CIIMAIROCIG 111 a few introduotory remarks said it was scarcely to be wondered at that in a variable climate such as ours the state of the weather formed a subject of remark and conversation under all kinds of circumstances, and to farmers and sailors it might be said to possess a sort of pro- fessional interest. The first practical application of the spectroscope as a means of foretelling rain appeared to have been made by Professor Piazzi Smyth, in the year 1872. Before this, however, and indeed from the time that Angstrom first published his maps of the solar spectrum it was known to observers that the presence or absence of certain dark lines or bands in the spectrum indicated the presence or otherwise of moisture, but Professor Smyth was the first to apply this knowledge practically, when in the year 11172 he predicted a destructive sirocco at Palermo from the appearance of the dark bands. The lecturer then went on to explain the construction of the epectroscope, and the manner in which it broke up white light into its con- stituent coloured elements and dispersed them in their invariable order as shown by the coloured diagrams which be used ti farther elucidate his subject. He ex- plained the appearances and position in the spectrum of what was termed the.rainband, which was always shown when there was a super-abundance of moisture in the atmosphere. With regard to the practical value of observations of this kind he could only say that his own experience was de- cidedly in favour of them. Taken alone they were only useful in forecasting changes for short periods and over limited areas, but when the indications ef the spectrum were combined with those of the barometer, and the direc- tion of the wind was also taken into account, reliable fore- casts for twelve hours in advance might be made after a few weeks practise. For the last three months he had made daily forecasts into which data derived from spectroscopic observations have daily entered. Mr. Sherrock also pro- duced the instrument with which his observations had been made, which was about three inches in length. The CHAIRMAN said the lecture had been given by Mr. Sherrock in A very clear and distinct manner. If there was anyone who wished to ask any questions he had no doubt the lecturer would be ready to answer them. For his own part, he should like to ask, as the spectroscope would fore- tell rain in a short time, how it would be when rain came from clouds in the atmosphere which had been brought there by a heavy gale from a distance of about fifty miles, in a short time perhaps after the observations had been taken. Would the spectroscope in that case be of any use In response to a request of the Chairman, Dr. MeNecon said he did not quite see why he should speak first except it was because he came in last. He thought the lecturer had hit the happy medium between two extremes. Some- times lecturers talked to their audiences as if they were babes, and sometimes they talked as if they were learned savants and scientists ; but the lecturer in the present instance had hit the happy medium between those two extremes. The subject was a novel one, and he did not think they could have much discussion because the thing was so new, but they were certainly very much indebted to ' Mr. Sherrock for bringing it forward. He thought himself that by collating the indications of the barometer and the hydrometer, which was generally attached, with the direction of the wind they could acquire as much certainty as was possible with regard to so fickle a thing as the weather. The rainband seemed to him to be a rival of the hydrometer in giving an ocular test as to whether there was moisture in the atmosphere or not. Dr. JAMISON suggested that the observations made by Mr. Sherrock should be placed up at the Town Hall or some other public place. The Rev. Mr. BROWN said he used to be able to forecast the weather pretty well by the look of the heavens, but since be came to St. Helens he had frequently not been able to get a look at the heavens. He was afraid some difficulty would attend the use of the spectroscope unless they went outside the town. Mr. SHEBROCE said with respect to the difficulties in the way of the use of the spectrum in cloudy and smokey weather, the difficulty applied to the whole of the spectrum. Fog or smoke in the atmosphere simply produced a dull spectrum, but did not make the slightest difference in the lines or rainbands. Then with respect to Dr. McNicoll's suggestion that the hydrometer attached to the barometer would answer the same purposes as the rainband, there were very few ordinary barometers fitted with the hydometer. Besides, the hydrometer eves an arrangement which required continual attention and observation to keep it in order and supply it with water, while it did not take half a minute to sweep the sky with the spectroscope and determine whether there was rain about, and, if so, its probable amount and duration. In respect to Dr. Jamison's suggestion, he could only say that he had hitherto put up outside his place of residence the results of his observations where they were publicly to be seen, and were closely studied by considerable numbers of people—(hear,, bear)—and their accuracy seemed to satisfy the intelligence of the Market- place at least. He bad known instances in which people who put up stalls in the market place have looked at the forecasts and afterwards packed up and gone elsewhere. (Laughter.) Any one wishing to study those forecasts could do 80 by looking at them where they were at present displayed just as easily as at the Town Hall. Speaking to the question of the Chairman, Mr. Sherrock said it was well known in St. Helens and neighbourhood that the south-west wind always brought rain. In cases of doubt when a person had occasion to go a journey and did not know whether to take an umbrella with him or not that an observation by the spectroscope very often cleared up the doubt. Of course it was always desirable when persons were going a distance that appearances and the direction of the wind should be

taken into account, but at the same time be had seen a die' dna rainband from a perfectly °tear sky in'which the slin was shining, and he knew, notwithstanding appearane"' that rain would follow very rapidly, and in most cases rain had followed within half an hour. A Tote of thanks to the Lecturer was accorded, On the motion of Mr. Simason (Cowley Schools), seconded by., councinv C. J. BISHOP, after which Mr. Sherrock eboW" his spectroscope to those present.
